title: The BA in a Bank Change Programme
one_screen: A banking BA turns a required business outcome into a chain of explicit requirements, decisions, approvals, acceptance and operational ownership. The BA makes the chain visible and durable, but does not absorb the accountability of the sponsor, business owner, project manager, architect, engineer, risk owner or production owner.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism The BA preserves meaning as work crosses organisational boundaries; documenting the change is only one part of that job. | Change point | BA contribution | Accountable owner | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Problem | Frame and test the need | Sponsor or business owner | | Requirement | Elicit, structure, trace | Requirement or process owner | | Design | Challenge against approved need | Architect or technology owner | | Evidence | Connect to requirement; expose gaps | Test, control or acceptance owner | | Go-live | Expose readiness and unresolved issues | Go/no-go authority | | Live outcome | Force explicit handover | BAU process or service owner | | Disputed decision | Frame options and consequences | Authorised decision-maker | | Missing owner | Surface and escalate the gap | Role holding the mandate | Facilitation never transfers accountability. Resolve an unowned decision before it becomes an implied BA choice, informal approval or production risk. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA produces structured requirements, decision records, traceability and impact analysis | | Approves | Business or control owners approve what falls within their mandate | | Consumes | Delivery, testing, operations, risk, finance and control teams consume the agreed meaning | | Independently challenges | Risk, compliance, model validation, internal audit or other independent functions where their mandate applies | ### Permanent rule Facilitation does not transfer accountability. Every material requirement, acceptance decision and residual risk needs a named owner with authority to own it. ### Never confuse [Facilitation] and [Accountability] **Facilitation** - frames the question, brings the right people together, records the decision and keeps the chain coherent. --- **Accountability** - carries the authority and consequence for the decision or outcome. ### Permanent trap The competent BA becomes the unofficial owner of everything because everyone relies on them. That feels efficient during delivery and fails at sign-off, go-live or audit because the person who prepared the decision was never authorised to make it. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Change Mandate, Deadline and Non-Negotiables
one_screen: Every banking change starts with a mandate: an external obligation, remediation commitment, strategic objective or operational need. Before requirements begin, the BA separates what must be achieved from what is merely the current preferred solution, and identifies which date, outcome and constraints are genuinely non-negotiable.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism A usable mandate separates what must be achieved from what delivery may still trade. | Element | Mandate must establish | | :--- | :--- | | Required outcome | Condition that must be true after change | | Trigger | Regulation, finding, strategy, incident or dependency | | Deadline | Setter and authority to move it: fixed external, internal commitment or target | | Mandatory scope | Work without which the outcome fails | | Discretionary scope | Improvement that can be traded without defeating the outcome | | Constraints | Calendar, platform, control, funding or resource limits | | Evidence | What must be demonstrable, and by whom | | Delivery pressure | Consequences for scope, resources, sequence and residual risk | Delivery difficulty does not move a date. Only the authority that set an external, executive or strategic commitment can change it. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA converts the initiating statement into explicit outcome, constraints and open questions | | Approves | Sponsor, business owner or accountable control owner confirms the mandate | | Consumes | Governance, delivery, architecture, testing and operations use it to judge later choices | | Independently challenges | Risk, compliance or internal audit challenge where the initiating obligation falls within their mandate | ### Permanent rule A deadline is fixed only because an authority outside the delivery team has made it fixed. The project cannot silently redefine the obligation to fit its plan. ### Never confuse [Mandate] and [Solution] **Mandate** - the outcome, obligation and constraints that must be satisfied. --- **Solution** - one proposed way of satisfying them. ### Permanent trap Starting detailed requirements from a solution name. "Build a new engine" can hide the real objective, preserve avoidable design assumptions and make later alternatives look like scope changes when the mandate never required that design. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. A specific regulator may impose a particular implementation date or evidence obligation, but the change discipline for interpreting it is the same.

title: Stakeholders, Mandates and Decision Rights
one_screen: A stakeholder list is not enough in a bank because people attend for different reasons and hold different authority. The BA must distinguish knowledge, impact, decision rights, approval rights, acceptance rights and challenge rights so that the loudest participant does not accidentally become the owner.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Map people by mandate, not title, visibility or meeting attendance. | Role | Owns or supplies | | :--- | :--- | | Need owner | Required business outcome | | SME | Process, rule or system knowledge; no automatic approval right | | Requirement owner | Meaning of the business obligation | | Decision authority | Choice between legitimate competing interests | | Approver | Formal approval within a defined mandate | | Acceptance authority | Fitness for business use and disclosed limitations | | Go/no-go authority | Permission to start production transition | | Residual-risk owner | Acceptance and monitoring of known post-release exposure | | Independent challenger | Challenge to risk or control weakness without first-line ownership | One person may hold several roles, but name each role separately because authority changes with the decision. Low attendance can coexist with veto authority; high visibility can coexist with none. Where policy owner and operator disagree, preserve both inputs until policy, practice and authority are reconciled. A reporting head may own need, requirement and acceptance without becoming architect or test owner. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA drafts the role and decision-right map | | Approves | Sponsor or programme governance confirms decision authorities | | Consumes | All workstreams use it to route questions, approvals and escalations | | Independently challenges | Control functions challenge omissions where their mandate is affected | ### Permanent rule Presence in a meeting is not authority. Authority comes from the role's organisational mandate and must be explicit before a material decision is treated as settled. ### Never confuse [SME] and [Decision authority] **SME** - provides deep knowledge about a process, rule, system or control. --- **Decision authority** - has the mandate to choose when options or stakeholder positions conflict. ### Permanent trap Writing "business to confirm" as an owner. "Business" is a population, not an accountable person or role; unresolved collective ownership becomes delayed sign-off and disputed decisions. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Governance Forums, Escalation and Decision Authority
one_screen: Bank change creates decisions that no single workstream can settle: business value may conflict with control expectations, technology feasibility with deadlines, or two functions may interpret the same obligation differently. Governance works when each question reaches the smallest forum that actually has authority to decide it.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Escalation is not failure. It is the mechanism for moving a decision to the correct level of authority. | Decision | Keep local when | Escalate when | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Requirement wording | Owner and SMEs agree within approved scope | Meaning changes obligation or creates cross-function conflict | | Design choice | Solution owner can satisfy agreed constraints | Choice changes business outcome, control or accepted risk | | Scope trade-off | Within delegated tolerance | Mandatory outcome, deadline or major dependency is affected | | Defect disposition | Existing tolerance clearly covers it | Release consequence or residual risk requires new acceptance | | Go-live readiness | Criteria are met | Criteria are waived, evidence is incomplete or material risk remains | The BA prepares escalation so governance receives a decision, not a data dump: issue, options, consequences, recommendation if appropriate, decision required, owner and latest decision date. The decision date matters because an answer delivered after build or test has already depended on it is not governance; it is retrospective documentation. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA frames decision papers and records outcomes | | Approves | Forum chair or authorised decision-maker approves within delegated mandate | | Consumes | Workstreams consume the decision and resulting constraints | | Independently challenges | Relevant control functions challenge decisions affecting their risk or control mandate | ### Permanent rule Every escalation must ask for a specific decision from a forum authorised to make it. Escalating information without a decision request creates visibility, not resolution. ### Never confuse [Escalation] and [Delegation] **Escalation** - moves a decision upward or across because the current owner lacks mandate, agreement or tolerance. --- **Delegation** - grants decision authority downward within defined boundaries. ### Permanent trap Using senior governance to settle every detailed question. That slows delivery and weakens accountability because people stop making decisions within their own mandate. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Problem Framing and Root Cause in Bank Change
one_screen: A reported problem is usually a symptom: a regulatory return breaks, reconciliations require manual repair, or an impairment run finishes too late. The BA frames the problem so the programme changes the causal mechanism rather than spending money to automate or relocate the symptom.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Separate the observed failure from the condition that allows it to recur. | Layer | Reporting example | BA test | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Symptom | Late manual adjustment | What failed or needed intervention? | | Immediate cause | Source arrived after freeze | What directly produced it? | | Contributing condition | Source timing owner unclear | What allowed it to persist? | | Root cause | No accountable cutoff control | What would prevent recurrence? | | Required outcome | Source completion owned and evidenced before freeze | What must become true? | | Evidence | Logs, steps, exceptions, reconciliations, decisions, workarounds | Does evidence support causality? | | Multiple causes | Several conditions contribute | Preserve the chain; do not force one neat cause | | Remediation | Today's output corrected | Was the enabling process or control weakness removed? | "Five whys" can prompt inquiry but does not prove causality. Correction restores today's output; remediation removes the recurring condition. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA structures the problem and evidence chain | | Approves | Business or control owner confirms the problem definition and required outcome | | Consumes | Delivery and design teams use it to avoid solving the wrong problem | | Independently challenges | Risk, compliance, operational risk or audit challenge root cause where relevant | ### Permanent rule A root cause must explain why the symptom occurred and identify something the change can act on. A label such as "human error" is not sufficient if the process made the error likely or undetectable. ### Never confuse [Symptom] and [Root cause] **Symptom** - the visible failure, delay, error or workaround that triggered attention. --- **Root cause** - the underlying controllable condition whose correction materially reduces recurrence. ### Permanent trap Writing the desired solution into the problem statement. "The problem is that we do not have platform X" closes solution space before the actual process or control failure has been established. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Discovering the As-Is Process and Control Reality
one_screen: The documented process is often cleaner than the live process. In banking change, the BA must discover the real sequence of work, decisions, controls, exceptions, handoffs and manual repairs because the hidden step is often the step that fails after migration or at period-end.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Reconstruct the present state before designing the future state, using evidence from both policy and operation. | Examine | What to establish | | :--- | :--- | | Trigger and inputs | What starts work and what must already exist | | Activities | What actually happens, in sequence | | Decisions | Who chooses, under which rule | | Handoffs | Where ownership moves | | Controls | What prevents or detects error | | Exceptions | What happens when normal flow fails | | Manual work | Spreadsheets, email or adjustments keeping the process alive | | Calendar | Day-end, month-end and reporting-cutoff differences | | Policy versus practice | Authorised process and reason for live deviation | | Evidence base | Documents, walkthroughs, observation and records | Seniority does not settle factual contradictions. Reconcile owner and operator accounts into an approved process, accepted workaround or explicit change problem; this also protects hidden controls and peak-period dependencies from being designed away. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA reconstructs and validates the as-is view | | Approves | Process owner confirms the governed baseline and known deviations | | Consumes | Requirements, design, testing and operations teams use the baseline | | Independently challenges | Control functions challenge omitted controls or unrecognised workarounds where relevant | ### Permanent rule A future-state design is unsafe until the current controls and exceptions are understood. Removing a manual step can remove a manual control at the same time. ### Never confuse [Documented process] and [Operating process] **Documented process** - the approved or described way work is intended to happen. --- **Operating process** - the way work is actually completed, including exceptions and workarounds. ### Permanent trap Treating undocumented work as irrelevant because it "should not happen". If the bank depends on it today, migration must either preserve the outcome or deliberately eliminate the dependency. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Eliciting from a Time-Pressed SME
one_screen: A banking SME may control twenty minutes of knowledge that the programme cannot safely guess. The BA earns that time by doing the document work first, asking questions that require expert judgement rather than lookup, and leaving with explicit confirmations, owners and unresolved points.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism The scarce resource is not meeting time; it is expert attention. | Before | During | After | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Read policies, existing requirements, reports and process evidence | State the decision or knowledge needed | Send a concise confirmation of conclusions | | Mark what is already known | Ask highest-risk questions first | Separate confirmed facts from assumptions | | Prepare scenarios and contradictions | Use concrete examples and exceptions | Assign unanswered questions to named owners | | Send a short pre-read | Reflect back the answer in business language | Record decisions in the durable log | | Know what can be answered without the SME | Stop when the required knowledge is obtained | Re-book only for genuinely new expert questions | A strong question is bounded: "When an account cures after the reporting cutoff, which status should the report use and who approves an override?" A weak question is "Can you explain the process?" Use scenario walkthroughs when rules are tacit. Ask for normal case, boundary case, failure case and override. If the SME says "it depends", the next question is what it depends on: a rule, judgement, system limitation, approval or convention. Do not force consensus from one SME where authority belongs elsewhere. Capture expert interpretation, then route the decision to the requirement owner or authorised forum. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA prepares questions, captures answers and distinguishes fact from interpretation | | Approves | Requirement or process owner approves conclusions requiring formal commitment | | Consumes | Delivery, design and testing teams consume clarified business knowledge | | Independently challenges | Relevant control functions challenge interpretations within their mandate | ### Permanent rule Never spend SME time discovering information available in documents you could have read. Use expert time for judgement, exceptions, ambiguity and decisions. ### Never confuse [Expert input] and [Formal approval] **Expert input** - explains how a rule, process, product or system works. --- **Formal approval** - commits an authorised owner to the requirement or decision. ### Permanent trap Leaving the meeting with notes but no distinction between what was confirmed, what was assumed and what remains open. Ambiguous notes become false requirements once circulated. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Conflicting Stakeholders and Requirement Negotiation
one_screen: Bank stakeholders can disagree while all being locally rational: operations wants speed, risk wants stronger controls, finance wants stable close, and technology wants a feasible design. The BA does not "find the middle"; the BA exposes the decision, evidence, consequences and authority so the conflict can be resolved without hiding the trade-off.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Separate disagreements by type before negotiating them. | Conflict type | What is really disputed | BA response | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Fact | What happens today or what evidence shows | Establish evidence | | Interpretation | What a rule or policy means | Obtain authoritative interpretation | | Objective | Which outcome matters more | Escalate to business authority | | Constraint | What is feasible by date or platform | Validate constraint and options | | Risk appetite | Which exposure may be accepted | Route to authorised risk owner | | Preference | Which option is more convenient | Decide against agreed criteria | Do not translate disagreement into vague wording that lets each side believe it won. A requirement that says "timely processing with appropriate controls" may conceal an unresolved cutoff, approval rule or tolerance. Write the unresolved decision explicitly. Where possible, create options that preserve mandatory outcomes while varying discretionary features, sequencing or operating model. If no option satisfies all mandates, the conflict belongs in governance. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA frames conflict, criteria, options and consequences | | Approves | Named decision authority selects the option | | Consumes | All affected stakeholders and delivery teams consume the recorded outcome | | Independently challenges | Control functions challenge options that weaken controls or exceed tolerances | ### Permanent rule Consensus is useful but authority is decisive. A material requirement is settled when the authorised owner decides, not when the meeting becomes quiet. ### Never confuse [Consensus] and [Decision] **Consensus** - participants broadly agree with an outcome. --- **Decision** - an authorised role commits the organisation to an outcome. ### Permanent trap Writing compromise language to avoid escalation. Ambiguity moves the conflict downstream, where developers, testers or operators make the decision accidentally. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Scope: In, Out, Assumed and Deferred
one_screen: Scope is a boundary around the outcome, not a list of things the project happens to discuss. A bank change is controllable only when in-scope obligations, explicit exclusions, assumptions and deliberately deferred work are all visible enough that later discovery cannot masquerade as an old commitment.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Four categories prevent most scope disputes. | Category | Meaning | Required discipline | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | In scope | Must be delivered in this change | Trace to requirements and acceptance | | Out of scope | Explicitly excluded | State why and confirm no mandatory outcome depends on it | | Assumed | Treated as true for current planning | Name owner and resolution date | | Deferred | Valid need intentionally moved to later delivery | Record authority, consequence and target owner | Scope should be bounded by business outcomes and affected capabilities, not by documents. "All fields in report X" is not sufficient if the change also alters upstream approval, reconciliation or production support. Use interfaces as scope tests: what enters the changed process, what leaves it, and which team owns each side? A system can be technically out of scope but operationally dependent on the change. That dependency belongs in impact analysis even if no build is planned there. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA structures scope and records boundary decisions | | Approves | Sponsor or accountable business owner approves scope baseline | | Consumes | Delivery, finance, governance, testing and operations use it to control commitments | | Independently challenges | Risk or compliance challenge exclusions that may undermine mandatory obligations | ### Permanent rule An exclusion is safe only if its effect on the required outcome is understood. "Out of scope" cannot be used to make a dependency disappear. ### Never confuse [Out of scope] and [Deferred] **Out of scope** - not part of the committed change. --- **Deferred** - a recognised need intentionally postponed, with an owner and consequence. ### Permanent trap Using assumptions as permanent scope shortcuts. An unresolved assumption can invalidate estimates, design and testing; if it matters, it needs an owner and resolution date. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Business Requirements and Business Rules
one_screen: A business requirement states the outcome or behaviour the business needs; a business rule states the condition that governs a decision, calculation, classification or action. The BA makes both precise enough to implement and accept without prescribing technical design that belongs to specialist solution owners.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Requirements become usable when each statement has one obligation, an owner and a clear condition of satisfaction. | Element | Requirement question | | :--- | :--- | | Actor or process | Who or what needs the capability? | | Required behaviour | What must happen? | | Trigger | When does it apply? | | Business rule | Under what condition or logic? | | Boundary | What cases are included or excluded? | | Constraint | What operational limit must hold? | | Owner | Who confirms the meaning? | | Acceptance condition | What evidence will show the need is met? | A lending migration requirement might say the servicing process must preserve the approved repayment schedule and account status through migration. The detailed source-to-target mapping is a data control owned elsewhere; BA carries only the business obligation and the impact of any mapping decision. A good rule is deterministic where the business is deterministic: "If condition X holds at cutoff, classify as Y." If judgement is intended, say who exercises it, what evidence they use and what approval applies. Do not convert real judgement into fake algorithmic precision. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA drafts and structures requirement statements and business rules | | Approves | Requirement owner confirms business meaning | | Consumes | Architecture, technology, data, testing and operations consume the approved obligation | | Independently challenges | Control functions challenge requirements affecting their mandate | ### Permanent rule A requirement states what must be true for the business; design states how the solution will make it true. Precision does not require the BA to take design ownership. ### Never confuse [Business requirement] and [Functional specification] **Business requirement** - states the required business outcome, behaviour, rule or constraint. --- **Functional specification** - states how solution components will implement that requirement. ### Permanent trap Hiding an unresolved decision inside passive language such as "appropriate", "where required" or "as necessary". If the condition matters to implementation or acceptance, define the rule or name the authority that decides it. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Operational and Non-Functional Constraints
one_screen: A banking change can be functionally correct and still be unusable because it misses the operating conditions under which the bank must run it. The BA captures operational and non-functional constraints as business obligations: availability, capacity, access, auditability, recoverability, support, processing windows and other qualities that determine whether the change works in production.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Treat each constraint as an observable condition, not an adjective. | Constraint | Weak wording | Decision-ready wording asks | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Availability | "Highly available" | During which business windows must service be available, and what interruption is tolerable? | | Performance | "Fast" | Which transaction or batch must finish by what operational cutoff? | | Capacity | "Scalable" | What volume, peak pattern and growth assumption must be supported? | | Access | "Secure" | Which roles may perform which actions, and who approves access? | | Auditability | "Fully auditable" | Which actions and decisions must leave retrievable evidence? | | Recoverability | "Resilient" | What business state must be restorable after failure and within what operating tolerance? | | Support | "Supported" | Who owns incidents, data questions and business decisions after go-live? | | Calendar | "Meets close" | Which day-end, month-end, quarter-end or filing cutoff must not be breached? | Specialist teams may translate these obligations into technical measures. BA owns the business meaning and the owner who can judge whether the constraint is sufficient. Do not manufacture numerical thresholds. If the business has not decided one, record an open decision rather than writing a convenient number into a requirement. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA elicits and structures business-facing constraints | | Approves | Service, process, control or business owner approves the required level | | Consumes | Architecture, technology, operations and testing translate constraints into implementation and evidence | | Independently challenges | Information security, operational risk, compliance or resilience functions challenge within mandate | ### Permanent rule If a quality matters to business acceptance, it is a requirement even when it is "non-functional". Unstated operational expectations are still capable of breaking go-live. ### Never confuse [Functional behaviour] and [Operational constraint] **Functional behaviour** - what the process or system must do. --- **Operational constraint** - the conditions under which that behaviour must remain usable, controlled and supportable. ### Permanent trap Assuming technology will "handle" capacity, logging, recovery or access later. Without business-defined needs, technical teams can implement a reasonable solution that is still wrong for close, control or support. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Assumptions, Open Questions and the Decision Log
one_screen: Unanswered questions do not disappear; they harden into assumptions inside design, estimates and test evidence. The BA keeps uncertainty visible by separating assumptions from facts, assigning every material open question to an owner, and recording decisions with enough context that the programme can later prove what was decided and why.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Use three distinct objects. | Object | Meaning | Minimum content | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Assumption | A proposition temporarily treated as true | Statement · impact if false · owner · resolution date | | Open question | Information or decision still required | Question · decision authority · due date · dependency | | Decision | An authorised choice that constrains future work | Decision · authority · date · rationale · consequences | A decision log is not meeting minutes. Minutes record discussion; the log records the outcome that delivery must rely on. Capture enough rationale to distinguish a conscious trade-off from an accidental omission. When a decision changes, do not overwrite history. Record the superseding decision and identify what earlier requirement, design, test or plan is affected. This makes traceability survive scope change. Time matters. An unanswered question needed before design freeze is different from one needed before go-live. The due date should be the latest safe decision point, not the next convenient committee meeting. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA records assumptions, open questions and durable decision entries | | Approves | Named decision authority approves each material decision | | Consumes | Delivery, testing, governance and operations rely on the current decision state | | Independently challenges | Control functions challenge assumptions or decisions within their mandate | ### Permanent rule Material uncertainty must have a visible state: unresolved, assumed, decided or superseded. It must never be allowed to look accidentally final. ### Never confuse [Decision log] and [Meeting minutes] **Decision log** - the durable record of authorised choices that constrain delivery. --- **Meeting minutes** - a record of discussion, actions and events in a meeting. ### Permanent trap Marking an issue "closed" because it was discussed. Closure requires either an authoritative answer or an accepted assumption with explicit consequences. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Requirements Sign-Off: Authority, Meaning and Evidence
one_screen: Requirements sign-off is not proof that a document was circulated; it is an authorised commitment to a defined baseline. The BA makes clear who is signing, what their signature means, what remains outside that commitment, and what durable evidence will survive later claims that approval was never given.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Sign-off has four dimensions. | Dimension | Required question | | :--- | :--- | | Authority | Is this person authorised to approve this requirement or baseline? | | Object | Exactly which version, requirements and assumptions are being approved? | | Meaning | Is the approver confirming business correctness, control adequacy, funding, design, or something else? | | Evidence | What durable record proves approval and its conditions? | A single "approved" status can conceal different commitments. A business owner may approve requirement meaning; a risk function may provide challenge or control approval; technology may confirm feasibility. Do not collapse those into one generic sign-off. Conditional approval must name the condition. "Approved subject to reconciliation evidence before go-live" is a real state; "approved with comments" is not useful unless the comments and ownership are explicit. After sign-off, clarification can still occur without reopening the baseline if it does not change meaning. A change to obligation, boundary, acceptance condition or constraint is a scope or requirement change and belongs in change control. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA prepares the baseline, approval statement and evidence trail | | Approves | Named requirement or control owners approve within their mandates | | Consumes | Delivery and governance rely on the approved baseline | | Independently challenges | Independent functions challenge whether required owners or conditions are missing | ### Permanent rule Sign-off commits an authorised person to a specific object and meaning. An email reaction, meeting attendance or silence is not equivalent unless the agreed governance explicitly makes it so. ### Never confuse [Sign-off] and [Acceptance] **Sign-off** - approves a requirement, scope, design input or other baseline before or during delivery. --- **Acceptance** - decides that the delivered change is suitable for business use against agreed evidence and disclosed limitations. ### Permanent trap Requesting approval with no statement of what approval means. Later disputes are often not about whether someone clicked "approve", but about whether they thought they were approving completeness, wording, feasibility or production readiness. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. A specific supervisory or internal governance process may impose particular evidence or approval requirements, but the discipline remains the same.

title: Traceability Through Change
one_screen: Traceability in BA is the survival of business meaning as requirements split, merge, change, defer and pass through specialist delivery artefacts. Data teams own the internal content of mapping and test-control artefacts; BA owns the chain that shows which mandate and approved requirement each delivery and acceptance decision serves.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism The minimum business chain is bidirectional. | Trace question | Why it matters | | :--- | :--- | | Why does this requirement exist? | Prevents orphan scope | | What changed its meaning? | Preserves decision history | | Which delivery item implements it? | Exposes missing implementation | | Which evidence supports acceptance? | Exposes untested or unevidenced obligations | | What happened if it was deferred? | Prevents silent loss | | Which requirement does this build item serve? | Exposes gold-plating and accidental scope | A data mapping specification must carry the data-control content needed for lineage; a test pack must carry the evidence mechanics needed for testing. BA does not duplicate those structures. BA keeps the business link into and out of them. Traceability must support versioning. If requirement R4 becomes R4a and R4b after a policy decision, preserve the relationship rather than deleting R4 and pretending the children always existed. Coverage is not just "every requirement has a link". A link to the wrong version or an obsolete test is false comfort. Status must reflect the current baseline. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA maintains business-level traceability and change relationships | | Approves | Requirement owners confirm material changes to meaning | | Consumes | Delivery, data, testing, governance and assurance teams use the chain | | Independently challenges | Assurance or control functions challenge gaps in required evidence or ownership | ### Permanent rule Traceability is about meaning, not hyperlinks. A complete-looking matrix is useless if it connects obsolete versions or artefacts that no longer prove the approved requirement. ### Never confuse [Traceability] and [Data lineage] **Traceability** - connects mandate, requirement, decision, delivery and acceptance through change. --- **Data lineage** - connects data origin, transformation and use so the movement and meaning of data can be followed. ### Permanent trap Rebuilding traceability just before acceptance. By then, scope decisions and version history have been lost, and the matrix becomes a reconstruction rather than a control. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Impact and Dependency Analysis
one_screen: A requirement can be small while its blast radius is large. Impact analysis follows the change across processes, controls, systems, data, reports, models, users, vendors, support teams and business-calendar dependencies so that an apparently local decision does not break an upstream source or downstream obligation.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Use a dependency lens, not only a system list. | Dimension | Questions | | :--- | :--- | | Process | Which activities, handoffs, cutoffs or exceptions change? | | People | Which roles perform, approve, support or rely on the process? | | Controls | Which preventive, detective or approval controls move or disappear? | | Systems | Which applications send, receive, calculate or store affected information? | | Data | Which sources, definitions, transformations or outputs are affected? | | Reports | Which management, finance or regulatory outputs consume the change? | | Models | Does the change alter a model input, output, use or operating process? | | Access | Which entitlements or segregation-of-duties patterns change? | | Calendar | Does cutover touch day-end, month-end, quarter-end or filing windows? | | Operations | Which incident, reconciliation or support process must change? | One-line specialist reminders are enough: model governance remains with MRM; statistical method with QNT; SQL/Python implementation with TEC; Indian regulatory substance with IND; data sourcing and mappings with DAT. Dependencies have direction. If system A feeds B, a format change in A affects B even when B is out of build scope. Record owner, dependency, impact and required action. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA coordinates cross-domain impact analysis and dependency record | | Approves | Affected owners confirm impacts within their domains | | Consumes | Planning, design, testing, operations and governance use identified dependencies | | Independently challenges | Risk and control functions challenge omitted control or risk impacts | ### Permanent rule Out of build scope does not mean out of impact scope. Anything the change can disrupt needs an owner and an assessed consequence. ### Never confuse [Scope] and [Impact] **Scope** - what the programme commits to change or deliver. --- **Impact** - everything whose behaviour, control, timing or outcome may be affected by that change. ### Permanent trap Asking only "which systems change?" A system-centric impact assessment misses operating procedures, controls, access, reporting calendars and manual reconciliations that can be equally critical to production safety. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Solution Challenge Without Solution Ownership
one_screen: The BA must challenge whether a proposed solution satisfies the approved business need without becoming the architect or engineer. The discipline is to test design decisions against requirements, constraints, impacts and operating reality, while leaving technical implementation accountability with the specialist owner.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Challenge the design through business consequences. | Design question | BA challenge | | :--- | :--- | | Coverage | Which approved requirements does this option satisfy, and which does it not? | | Assumptions | What business assumption does the design depend on? | | Exceptions | What happens outside the normal path? | | Controls | Which existing control is preserved, moved, automated or removed? | | Dependencies | Which upstream or downstream process changes because of this choice? | | Operations | How will users support, reconcile and recover the solution? | | Evidence | What will later demonstrate that the business obligation is met? | | Trade-off | What business outcome, risk or deadline changes if this option is chosen? | A BA can describe a business rule in enough detail to remove ambiguity. That does not make the BA owner of SQL, Python, database structures, API design or source-to-target mappings. TEC owns SQL and Python implementation; DAT owns data-control specifications. The BA should ask whether those artefacts preserve the approved business meaning. When a proposed design cannot satisfy a requirement, do not quietly rewrite the requirement to fit feasibility. Surface the gap as a decision: change solution, change requirement through authorised control, or accept the consequence through the correct owner. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Solution owner produces design; BA produces requirement and impact challenge | | Approves | Architecture or technology authority approves solution design within mandate | | Consumes | Build, data, testing and operations teams consume the design | | Independently challenges | Control functions challenge design impacts within their mandates | ### Permanent rule The BA may challenge the "how" because the "how" can violate the "what". Challenging a design does not transfer design accountability to the BA. ### Never confuse [Requirement clarification] and [Solution design] **Requirement clarification** - removes ambiguity from the business obligation without changing its approved meaning. --- **Solution design** - chooses the technical or operational mechanism used to satisfy that obligation. ### Permanent trap Accepting "the system cannot do that" as an automatic requirement change. Technical constraint is an input to a business decision, not authority to rewrite the need. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Baselines, Scope Change and Change Control
one_screen: Once scope and requirements are approved, later changes must preserve the history of what was committed and why it changed. Change control is not bureaucracy around wording; it is the mechanism that prevents a new obligation, exclusion or constraint from entering delivery without visible impact and authorised ownership.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Classify the incoming request before opening change control. | Incoming item | Meaning | Treatment | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Clarification | Same approved meaning, expressed more clearly | Update wording with traceable confirmation | | Correction | Baseline inaccurately captured already-approved meaning | Correct with owner evidence | | Scope change | Adds, removes or moves committed outcome | Impact assessment and approval | | Requirement change | Alters behaviour, rule, boundary or acceptance condition | Impact assessment and approval | | Design change | Alters solution while requirement remains stable | Solution governance; BA assesses business impact | | Defect | Delivered behaviour fails agreed expectation | Defect process; release consequence assessed separately | For a material change, assess effect before approval: mandate, requirements, design, data, testing, controls, dependencies, cost, schedule, readiness and evidence. The answer may be "no impact" for some dimensions, but it should be considered rather than assumed. Never replace the prior baseline. Preserve what was approved, the approved change and which downstream artefacts must be revisited. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA documents business change and coordinates impact assessment | | Approves | Scope or requirement authority approves within mandate | | Consumes | Delivery, testing, governance and operations consume the revised baseline | | Independently challenges | Risk or control functions challenge changes affecting their mandates | ### Permanent rule A baseline is allowed to change; it is not allowed to change invisibly. Material changes require preserved history, assessed consequences and authorised approval. ### Never confuse [Scope change] and [Requirement clarification] **Scope change** - changes what outcome or obligation is committed. --- **Requirement clarification** - makes the existing approved meaning clearer without changing the obligation. ### Never confuse [Defect] and [Change request] **Defect** - delivered behaviour fails an agreed requirement or expected result. --- **Change request** - proposes a different requirement, scope or solution from the current approved baseline. ### Permanent trap Calling a late request a "clarification" to avoid governance. If it changes expected behaviour, acceptance conditions, boundaries or constraints, it changes the baseline regardless of the label. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: The Immovable Deadline: Scope, Resources and Risk
one_screen: When a required implementation date cannot move, time stops being the balancing variable. The programme must make explicit choices among mandatory outcome, discretionary scope, sequencing, credible capacity and accepted risk rather than pretending the original plan remains achievable.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Protect the mandatory outcome first; then choose among delivery levers without hiding their cost. | Lever | Valid use | Boundary | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | De-scope | Discretionary, separable work | Mandatory obligations stay mandatory | | Re-sequence | Stages preserve the required end-state | Incomplete dependency is not a harmless phase | | Add resources | Work is parallelisable and capacity arrives in time | Onboarding and coordination can consume the gain | | Simplify | Simpler design still meets requirement and controls | Lower quality is not simplification | | Temporary control | Exposure is understood, time-bounded and owned | Workaround is not the target state | | Escalate | No credible plan meets date and obligation | Red status exposes the conflict; it does not solve it | | Decision pack | Authority must choose | Show requirement, outcome, control, dependency, evidence gap, owner and decision date | This makes consequences comparable and prevents "protect the date" from becoming permission to conceal unfinished mandatory work. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA frames scope and consequence options; project management supplies delivery capacity and schedule evidence | | Approves | Sponsor and relevant business or risk authorities approve trade-offs within mandate | | Consumes | Delivery, testing and operations execute the revised priorities | | Independently challenges | Control functions challenge weakened controls, unsupported deferrals or residual risk | ### Permanent rule A fixed deadline does not make all other constraints disappear. It forces earlier, clearer decisions about what is protected, what is deferred and who owns the resulting risk. ### Never confuse [Priority] and [Mandatory scope] **Priority** - the order in which work should receive attention. --- **Mandatory scope** - the minimum outcome that must be delivered for the governing obligation to be satisfied. ### Permanent trap Adding people as the default recovery plan. Late capacity helps only where work can be separated, knowledge transfer is feasible and coordination cost does not consume the gain. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The actual date or externally required evidence can vary by authority; the delivery discipline does not.

title: Iterative Delivery Without Losing Regulatory Completeness
one_screen: A bank may deliver through sequential phases, agile iterations or a hybrid, but the control invariant is the same: mandatory scope, decision authority, traceability, evidence and final business acceptance must survive the delivery method. Iteration changes how work is sliced; it does not make obligations optional or ownership informal.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Separate delivery cadence from governance completeness. | Delivery practice | Safe when | Failure mode | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Incremental build | Each increment traces to approved scope | Stories become the only source of requirement truth | | Evolving detail | Detail clarifies within authorised boundaries | Scope changes enter as backlog refinement | | Demonstrations | Feedback is captured and routed to decisions | Demo comments are mistaken for formal approval | | Backlog reprioritisation | Mandatory coverage remains protected | Low-visibility obligations continually slip | | Sprint acceptance | Increment meets its agreed conditions | Local acceptance is mistaken for final business acceptance | | Hybrid gates | Gates protect material decisions and evidence | Ceremony exists without a real decision right | A user story may be useful to a delivery team, but it is not automatically the full regulatory or business obligation. The BA maintains the relationship between slices and the approved baseline so that the programme can prove completeness at the end. "Agile" never means material decisions can remain oral. If a decision changes scope, control or acceptance, record and approve it through the same authority model used elsewhere. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Delivery teams produce increments; BA maintains business completeness and decision continuity | | Approves | Requirement and scope owners approve material changes | | Consumes | Product, project, technology, testing and governance teams use the shared baseline | | Independently challenges | Control functions challenge gaps in mandatory coverage or evidence | ### Permanent rule Methodology can change the rhythm of delivery, not the existence of accountability. Every mandatory obligation still needs an owner, implementation, evidence and acceptance. ### Never confuse [Sprint acceptance] and [Business acceptance] **Sprint acceptance** - confirms that an increment meets its local agreed conditions. --- **Business acceptance** - authorises the delivered change for business use against the complete approved obligation and disclosed limitations. ### Permanent trap Allowing backlog tools to become a substitute for governed scope. A backlog can organise work brilliantly while still losing the link to why the bank had to change. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Test Governance and Evidence Handoffs
one_screen: BA does not own the structure of test packs or the mechanics of UAT evidence; those are data and testing controls. BA owns the change discipline around testing: whether the requirement is ready to test, who supplies business truth, whether evidence maps to the current requirement, and how gaps are escalated before acceptance.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Testing needs governed handoffs, not only execution. | Handoff | BA question | Owner outside BA | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Requirement to test design | Is the current requirement unambiguous and approved? | Test owner designs coverage | | Business rule to expected result | Who can state the correct business outcome? | SME or requirement owner supplies truth | | Data need to test data | What business scenario must be represented? | Data/test team prepares controlled data | | Test result to requirement | Does the evidence address the current approved requirement? | Test owner records result | | Evidence gap to governance | What acceptance decision is blocked by missing evidence? | Decision authority resolves or accepts consequence | DAT owns what a test strategy, test pack and UAT evidence set must contain for data-control purposes. BA carries a one-line reminder of those objects and focuses on readiness, ownership, traceability and decision consequence. A requirement is not test-ready because it has been signed off if key rules remain assumed. Conversely, testing can reveal a requirement ambiguity rather than a software defect. Classify that outcome correctly before raising a defect or changing scope. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Test owners produce test artefacts; BA produces requirement clarification and evidence linkage | | Approves | Test governance approves test readiness and completion; requirement owners approve business meaning | | Consumes | Business acceptance and release governance consume the evidence | | Independently challenges | Assurance or control functions challenge evidence sufficiency where mandated | ### Permanent rule Test evidence is useful only against the current approved requirement. Passing obsolete requirements is not evidence that the bank is ready to accept the change. ### Never confuse [Test evidence] and [Acceptance decision] **Test evidence** - demonstrates observed results against defined conditions. --- **Acceptance decision** - an authorised business judgement that the delivered change is suitable for use given the evidence and known limitations. ### Permanent trap Letting testers decide ambiguous business rules because execution needs an answer. That converts a test assumption into an undocumented requirement decision. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Defects, Release Blockers and Residual-Risk Decisions
one_screen: A defect becomes a BA concern when it creates a business decision: does it violate a mandatory requirement, block an operating process, weaken a control, require a workaround or leave risk that someone must own at release? DAT owns defect-record, retest and closure mechanics; BA owns the requirement, impact and release consequence around that record.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Move from defect description to disposition decision. | Question | Why it matters | | :--- | :--- | | What requirement or expected behaviour failed? | Separates defect from enhancement | | Which process or output is affected? | Establishes business consequence | | Is mandatory scope compromised? | Determines whether release can satisfy mandate | | Is there a controlled workaround? | Tests temporary operability | | What control or evidence is weakened? | Makes hidden risk visible | | By when can it be fixed and retested? | Connects defect to release timing | | Who can accept the residual exposure? | Prevents project team from self-accepting risk | Severity and priority can inform the discussion, but labels do not make the decision. A technically minor issue can be a release blocker if it invalidates a required disclosure; a severe issue in an unused deferred component may have a different release consequence. If the proposed "fix" changes approved behaviour, it is also a change request and must follow change control. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Test team records defect; BA links it to requirement and business impact | | Approves | Product, business, control or release authority decides disposition within mandate | | Consumes | Delivery, testing, operations and go/no-go governance consume the decision | | Independently challenges | Risk or control functions challenge unacceptable residual exposure | ### Permanent rule A project team cannot make risk disappear by changing a defect status. Release with a known limitation requires an authorised owner for the resulting business or control exposure. ### Never confuse [Defect] and [Change request] **Defect** - the delivered solution does not meet the current approved expectation. --- **Change request** - proposes to alter the approved expectation or scope. ### Never confuse [Severity] and [Release consequence] **Severity** - a classification of the defect's impact under the defect scheme. --- **Release consequence** - the decision about whether and under what conditions the change may proceed to production. ### Permanent trap Using "workaround available" as automatic permission to release. The workaround itself has capacity, control, evidence, training and duration consequences that must be assessed. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Business Acceptance and the Meaning of UAT Sign-Off
one_screen: Business acceptance is the authorised judgement that the delivered change is suitable for business use against the approved requirements, available evidence and disclosed limitations. UAT evidence informs that judgement, but a collection of passed tests does not itself decide who accepts the changed process or what residual risk is being taken.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Acceptance combines evidence with authority. | Acceptance dimension | Required question | | :--- | :--- | | Authority | Who is authorised to accept the changed business capability? | | Baseline | Which requirement and scope version is being accepted? | | Evidence | Which test, reconciliation, readiness and control evidence supports the decision? | | Exceptions | Which requirements are not fully evidenced or met? | | Limitations | Which workarounds, defects or temporary controls remain? | | Conditions | What must happen before or after release? | | Residual risk | Who owns each known exposure? | DAT owns UAT coverage and business evidence as a data control. BA does not restate test-case mechanics; BA ensures the acceptance authority knows what the evidence proves, what it does not prove, and which open items are being consciously accepted. A single business sign-off may be insufficient where different owners hold different mandates. The reporting owner may accept business output while operations accepts process readiness and a risk owner accepts a temporary control. Combine those decisions only if the governance model gives one role authority over all of them. Conditional acceptance must be actionable: condition, owner, due date and consequence if unmet. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA assembles the acceptance decision view and links evidence to obligations | | Approves | Named business acceptance authority accepts within mandate | | Consumes | Release governance, operations and production owners rely on the acceptance | | Independently challenges | Risk, compliance or assurance challenge acceptance gaps within their mandates | ### Permanent rule Acceptance is a decision by an authorised owner, not a test status. Evidence supports acceptance; it does not replace accountability. ### Never confuse [Sign-off] and [Acceptance] **Sign-off** - approves an earlier baseline, requirement or delivery artefact within a defined mandate. --- **Acceptance** - authorises use of the delivered change against current evidence and known limitations. ### Permanent trap Asking business users to "sign UAT" without telling them whether they are confirming test execution, requirement coverage, operational readiness or production acceptance. Different commitments need different authority. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Where an authority requires specific implementation evidence, that evidence becomes an input to acceptance but does not change the ownership discipline.

title: Parallel Run, Coexistence and Migration Confidence
one_screen: A parallel run operates old and new states together so the bank can compare outcomes under live-like conditions before relying solely on the new process. BA owns why coexistence is needed, which business discrepancies matter, who resolves them and what exit decision ends the parallel period; DAT owns detailed downstream extract-validation mechanics.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Parallel run, dry run and phased cutover answer different transition questions. | Pattern | What it tests | Limitation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Parallel run | Old and new states on comparable live periods | Dual people, controls and reconciliation burden | | Dry run | Timing, roles and execution sequence without authoritative transition | Does not prove sustained live equivalence | | Phased cutover | Controlled movement by valid population, process or capability slice | Hidden dependencies can make a phase incomplete, not safer | | Parallel-run decision | Define before starting | | :--- | :--- | | Purpose and scope | Uncertainty, populations, outputs and periods being compared | | Tolerance | Expected, explainable and unacceptable differences | | Ownership | Who investigates and decides each discrepancy class | | Duration | Meaningful cycles that must be observed | | Exit | Who decides evidence is sufficient for replacement | | Fallback | Whether the old state can still support production | Identical outputs are unnecessary when approved logic, policy or timing changes; differences must instead be understood and authorised. QNT owns statistics, MRM model governance, and DAT detailed extract validation. BA owns the business comparison, discrepancy decision, temporary operating burden and exit authority. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA defines business comparison questions and discrepancy ownership with relevant teams | | Approves | Business or transition authority approves exit criteria and completion | | Consumes | Release governance and production owners use the confidence evidence | | Independently challenges | Risk, finance, model or control functions challenge unexplained differences within mandate | ### Permanent rule A parallel run is complete when its defined uncertainty has been reduced enough for an authorised exit decision, not merely when a calendar period ends. ### Never confuse [Parallel run] and [Dry run] **Parallel run** - old and new operating states run against comparable activity so outcomes can be assessed side by side. --- **Dry run** - a rehearsal of process, cutover or execution steps without necessarily operating both states as live alternatives. ### Permanent trap Declaring success because aggregate totals are close. Material population-level, control or classification differences can cancel out in totals and still make the new process unsafe. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Operational Readiness and the Banking Calendar
one_screen: A system can pass testing while the business is still not ready to operate it. Operational readiness proves that people, procedures, access, controls, support, reconciliations, communications and critical calendar dependencies are prepared for day one and for the high-risk cycles that follow.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Readiness is a set of owned operating conditions. | Readiness area | Evidence question | | :--- | :--- | | People | Are the required roles staffed and aware of new responsibilities? | | Procedures | Are operating and exception procedures current and usable? | | Access | Do users and support teams have approved entitlements? | | Controls | Are new or changed controls assigned, executable and evidenced? | | Reconciliation | Can outputs be checked and breaks owned? | | Support | Is incident, query and escalation ownership live? | | Training | Can affected users perform the changed process? | | Communications | Do dependent teams know what changes and when? | | Calendar | Has the release been assessed against close, filing and peak processing? | | Contingency | Can the business operate if a key component fails? | Month-end matters because operational tolerance changes. A credit migration that is safe on a quiet Tuesday may be unsafe before statement production, provisioning, finance close or a reporting cutoff. The BA does not impose a universal blackout calendar; the BA identifies which business events make the chosen date risky and who may accept that risk. Readiness should distinguish "complete" from "waived". A missing procedure signed off as a controlled temporary condition is not the same state as a completed procedure. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA coordinates readiness evidence; each operational owner produces domain evidence | | Approves | Business and service owners approve readiness within their areas | | Consumes | Go/no-go authority uses the integrated readiness view | | Independently challenges | Operational risk, compliance or control functions challenge material gaps | ### Permanent rule "System ready" and "business ready" are different states. Production transition requires both, plus explicit ownership of any waived readiness condition. ### Never confuse [Readiness gap] and [Defect] **Readiness gap** - an operating prerequisite such as training, access, procedure or support is incomplete. --- **Defect** - delivered behaviour fails an agreed requirement or expected result. ### Permanent trap Treating training completion percentages as proof of readiness. Attendance does not prove that critical roles can execute new decisions, controls and exceptions. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Cutover, Go/No-Go and Fallback Authority
one_screen: Cutover is the controlled transition from the old operating state to the new one. The BA's role is to make decision conditions and ownership explicit: what must be true before starting, who can proceed or stop, what business checks determine success, and who controls fallback if the transition becomes unsafe.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Cutover governance must distinguish the decision to go, the trigger to stop and the conditions for fallback. | State | Condition | Authority or action | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Go | Acceptance, readiness, access, data and support criteria met or waived | Go/no-go authority starts transition | | Continue | Business checkpoint passes | Cutover lead proceeds | | Stop | Defined trigger breaches tolerance or creates unsafe uncertainty | Stop authority halts sequence | | Fallback | New state is unsafe and fallback remains viable | Restore coherent business state | | Complete | Final checkpoints pass and ownership is clear | Declare cutover complete; hand to stabilisation | | Communicate | State, delay or fallback affects others | Inform users, executives, dependencies and support | Technology and data owners own detailed migration steps; BA owns the business checkpoints and dependencies they must protect. Fallback covers transactions, reconciliation, procedures, controls and reversals, not merely infrastructure. Agree criteria, authorities and permitted waivers before the go/no-go meeting. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Technology/data teams produce execution plan; BA integrates business checkpoints and decision conditions | | Approves | Named go/no-go authority authorises production transition | | Consumes | Cutover command, operations, support and business owners execute decisions | | Independently challenges | Risk or control functions challenge unresolved material readiness or fallback gaps | ### Permanent rule Go-live authority must be named before cutover begins, including who can stop the transition. Ambiguous authority becomes most dangerous when time pressure is highest. ### Never confuse [Go-live] and [Stabilisation] **Go-live** - the transition point at which the new state becomes production-active. --- **Stabilisation** - the controlled period after go-live in which production behaviour, incidents and temporary controls are monitored before normal support is declared. ### Permanent trap Treating fallback as a technical-only plan. If business state, transactions, controls and user procedures cannot be restored coherently, the fallback is not operationally viable. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Hypercare, Stabilisation and BAU Handover
one_screen: Go-live does not end the change; it starts the period in which production evidence replaces test assumptions. Hypercare is temporary enhanced support, stabilisation is the evidence-based judgement that the new state behaves within agreed tolerances, and BAU handover transfers enduring ownership away from the programme.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism The exit from project mode should be controlled like entry to production. | Stabilisation question | Required evidence | | :--- | :--- | | Are critical processes completing? | Production outcomes and cutoff performance | | Are incidents understood? | Trend, root cause and ownership | | Are reconciliations stable? | Break volumes, ageing and resolution | | Are temporary controls working? | Execution evidence and exceptions | | Can BAU support the service? | Named support route and knowledge transfer | | Are users operating without project dependency? | Reduced project intervention | | Are open defects and actions owned? | BAU owner, target date and escalation route | | Can hypercare end? | Exit criteria approved by service/business owner | Do not let the programme become permanent shadow support. If users still need developers or project SMEs for normal decisions, the operating model is not fully handed over. Production incidents can reveal requirements, design or training gaps. Classify them rather than reopening project scope automatically. A defect follows defect governance; a new need follows change control; an operating issue belongs to the BAU process owner. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Programme and BAU teams produce stabilisation evidence; BA tracks unresolved ownership | | Approves | Business or service owner approves hypercare exit and handover | | Consumes | BAU operations, support, risk and control teams inherit enduring obligations | | Independently challenges | Control functions challenge premature closure of material temporary controls or issues | ### Permanent rule Handover is complete when BAU can operate, support and own the changed process without hidden dependence on the project team. ### Never confuse [Hypercare] and [BAU support] **Hypercare** - temporary enhanced support immediately after production transition. --- **BAU support** - the enduring operating model that owns incidents, decisions, maintenance and controls after stabilisation. ### Permanent trap Using low incident count as the only stabilisation criterion. Some failures are silent and appear first in reconciliation, close, exception handling or delayed downstream processes. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.

title: Post-Implementation Review, Benefits and Closure
one_screen: A banking change is not complete because the release succeeded or the project budget closed. Post-implementation review asks whether the required outcome and promised benefits actually exist in production, whether controls operate as intended, and whether every residual action, temporary measure and accepted risk has a durable owner outside the programme.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Closure tests the original mandate against production reality and prevents unfinished obligations from becoming ownerless. | Review dimension | Closure test | | :--- | :--- | | Required outcome | Original mandate works in operation | | Requirements | Accepted requirements function in production | | Benefits | Mandated efficiency, quality, control, service or compliance outcome appears | | Controls | Changed controls operate and are evidenced | | Residual defects | Owner, date and escalation exist | | Temporary controls | Reason, owner and exit plan remain valid | | Accepted risks | Owners monitor what they accepted | | Dependencies | Delayed or downstream impacts are addressed | | Decisions | Material approval and change history are preserved | | Ownership | No material obligation is orphaned | | Minor open actions | Safe BAU transfer has owner, due date and escalation route | Benefits come from the mandate, not post-hoc success metrics: regulatory change may primarily deliver compliance; migration may reduce operational risk or remove unsupported infrastructure. Closure can precede minor action completion, but not transfer without durable accountability. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | BA assembles trace from mandate to production outcome and residual actions | | Approves | Sponsor or accountable business owner approves programme closure | | Consumes | BAU owners, governance and assurance functions consume the final evidence | | Independently challenges | Risk, compliance, internal audit or other assurance challenge closure where their mandate applies | ### Permanent rule The programme can close with open work only when every material open obligation has transferred to an accountable owner who has accepted it. ### Never confuse [Project closure] and [Outcome realisation] **Project closure** - ends the temporary delivery organisation and its governance. --- **Outcome realisation** - confirms that the required business, control or strategic result exists and continues in production. ### Permanent trap Archiving the project while temporary controls and deferred actions still depend on programme names or mailing lists. Once the programme disappears, those obligations become orphaned. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Where an external authority requires specific post-implementation evidence, that requirement becomes part of the closure evidence set.

title: Why Regulatory Capital Exists
one_screen: Expected loss is the centre of a loss distribution; unexpected loss is the adverse loss beyond that centre. IMP-01 → a loss allowance reduces an asset's carrying amount, while capital is loss-absorbing resource against unexpected loss. Regulatory capital exists to preserve solvency when realised losses outrun earnings and recognised loss allowances.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Object | Prudential job | | :--- | :--- | | Expected loss | Anticipated cost of taking risk | | Allowance | Recognised reduction in an asset's carrying amount | | Earnings | First recurring source for absorbing costs and rebuilding capital | | Regulatory capital | Loss-bearing resource protecting solvency against adverse outcomes | Basel's IRB architecture makes the split visible: its risk-weight functions are calibrated to unexpected loss, while regulatory expected loss is compared separately with eligible provisions. The split is conceptual, not a claim that accounting allowance must equal regulatory expected loss. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Capital is a solvency resource against loss. It is not a substitute for recognising expected credit losses promptly. ### Never confuse [Allowance] and [Capital] **Allowance** — a measured reduction in the carrying amount of an asset for recognised credit loss. --- **Capital** — qualifying loss-absorbing resource available to bear losses and preserve solvency. ### Permanent trap Calling an allowance "capital set aside for bad loans" collapses two different objects. The allowance changes the asset and earnings; capital is the residual loss-bearing claim after those accounting effects. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The loss-distribution logic is common; accounting and prudential implementation determine how the two objects interact.

title: Loss Absorption: Going Concern to Resolution
one_screen: FND-04 → capital is not liquidity: capital absorbs losses; liquidity meets payments when due. Within capital itself, timing matters: going-concern resources absorb loss while the bank remains viable, while gone-concern resources support creditor protection and resolution after viability is lost.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Basel classifies CET1 and AT1 within Tier 1, its going-concern layer. Tier 2 is the lower-quality layer intended principally for loss absorption at non-viability or resolution. The legal trigger and write-down or conversion mechanism depend on the applicable instrument terms and resolution law. A solvent bank can still be illiquid, and an illiquid bank can temporarily remain solvent. Therefore a strong CET1 ratio does not mean the bank holds enough cash to meet tomorrow's withdrawals. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Regulatory quality depends on whether loss absorption is reliably available when required, not on whether an instrument is called equity or subordinated debt. ### Never confuse [Going-concern capital] and [Gone-concern capital] **Going-concern capital** — absorbs loss while the institution remains viable and operating. --- **Gone-concern capital** — absorbs loss principally after non-viability, failure or resolution action. ### Permanent trap Treating Tier 2 as equivalent to CET1 because both count in Total Capital ignores the timing and quality of their loss absorption. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the Basel hierarchy. Resolution statutes and contractual non-viability mechanisms differ by jurisdiction.

title: The Capital Quality Hierarchy
one_screen: Regulatory capital is nested by quality. CET1 is the highest-quality layer; CET1 plus AT1 is Tier 1; Tier 1 plus Tier 2 is Total Capital. Because the categories are nested, lower-quality capital cannot repair a shortfall in a higher-quality requirement.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Layer | What it contributes | Can satisfy | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | CET1 | Highest-quality, permanent going-concern loss absorption | CET1, Tier 1 and Total Capital requirements | | AT1 | Additional going-concern capacity meeting stricter permanence and loss-absorption rules than ordinary debt | Tier 1 and Total Capital, not CET1 | | Tier 2 | Lower-quality subordinated gone-concern capacity | Total Capital only | Basel global minimum ratios are themselves nested: 4.5% CET1, 6% Tier 1 and 8% Total Capital, before buffers and any jurisdictional or firm-specific additions. A bank therefore does not add 4.5 + 6 + 8 and hold 18.5% merely because three ratios are reported. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Capital quality nests upward: CET1 can meet a broader requirement, but Tier 2 cannot meet a CET1 or Tier 1 shortfall. ### Never confuse [Tier 1] and [Total Capital] **Tier 1** — CET1 plus eligible AT1. --- **Total Capital** — Tier 1 plus eligible Tier 2. ### Permanent trap Adding the CET1, Tier 1 and Total Capital minimum percentages as separate capital layers triple-counts the same higher-quality capital. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the hierarchy. Jurisdictions may set higher ratios or additional layers above the Basel minima.

title: Common Equity Tier 1
one_screen: CET1 is the highest-quality regulatory capital because it bears losses continuously and is not protected by a contractual promise of repayment. FND-03 → retained earnings accumulate profit after distributions; losses run through earnings and therefore reduce CET1 unless another qualifying capital action offsets them.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism CET1 begins with qualifying common equity instruments, associated share premium, retained earnings and other eligible disclosed reserves, then applies prudential criteria and adjustments. | CET1 property | Why it matters | | :--- | :--- | | Perpetual | No maturity that forces repayment | | Most subordinated claim | Losses reach common equity before senior creditors | | Distributions discretionary | Bank is not forced to pay a coupon or dividend | | Fully available for loss absorption | Capital can fall as losses are recognised | | Clear issue and repayment rules | Prevents capital disappearing through redemption | A common share can fail regulatory eligibility if its terms weaken permanence or loss absorption.
