Filing rights and later committee voting are separate statutory questions. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Corporate persons Corporate insolvency runs through the National Company Law Tribunal architecture. #### Individuals and other debtor categories Different insolvency/recovery provisions and forums can apply; this atom does not import the corporate process automatically.

title: Recovery Conduct, Recovery Agents and Escalation
one_screen: Indian lenders remain responsible for how overdue debt is collected, including conduct by outsourced recovery agents. Recovery rights do not authorise intimidation, public shaming, misleading representations or uncontrolled contact; borrower grievance and RBI ombudsman routes remain available even when the account is genuinely in default.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Recovery control | Required outcome | | :--- | :--- | | Agent due diligence and authorisation | Lender knows who acts on its behalf | | Identity and communication discipline | Borrower can identify the lender/agent and reason for contact | | Contact controls | Recovery activity occurs within permitted conduct boundaries | | No harassment or intimidation | Default does not remove dignity and fair-treatment obligations | | Complaint handling | Borrower can escalate misconduct to the regulated entity | | Ombudsman route | Eligible unresolved service grievances can move to RBI's external redress framework | The lender cannot outsource accountability. If an agent breaches conduct rules, the regulated entity faces supervisory and customer-redress consequences. RBI issued recovery-conduct amendments on 6 August 2026 with an effective date of 1 January 2027. As at 31 August 2026 those future-effective provisions are not yet in force. This atom therefore distinguishes the current conduct framework from the 2027 amendments and does not backdate future requirements. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A valid debt does not legalise abusive collection. The lender is accountable for outsourced recovery conduct. ### Never confuse [Recovery right] and [Recovery method] **Recovery right** — the creditor's lawful claim to collect or enforce the debt. --- **Recovery method** — the manner in which collection is carried out; it remains subject to RBI conduct rules. ### Permanent trap Treating a third-party recovery agent as outside the lender's compliance perimeter. Outsourcing the call or visit does not outsource regulatory responsibility. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Banks, NBFCs and other covered REs Apply the conduct and outsourcing requirements relevant to their entity class. #### Future position from 1 January 2027 RBI's 6 August 2026 recovery-conduct amendments become effective; they are future rules as at 31 August 2026 and are not treated as currently operative.

title: What Counts as a Model
one_screen: A model is a governed representation that transforms inputs into outputs using assumptions and quantitative or cognitive techniques. Classification is consequential: model status brings inventory, validation, approval, monitoring and change controls, while the legal boundary differs materially across jurisdictions.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Test | Question | | :--- | :--- | | Inputs | Does it consume data, estimates, judgement or structured inputs? | | Transformation | Does it apply statistical, mathematical, economic, financial or comparable analytical assumptions or techniques? | | Output | Does it estimate, predict, classify, rank, optimise or inform a decision? | | Uncertainty | Can data, assumptions or method make the output wrong even when implementation is correct? | | Use | Does output affect business, risk, reporting, capital, customer or operational decisions? | Model classification follows substance, not software: ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Tool/model owner | Proposes classification and documents function and use | | MRM function | Challenges boundary decisions | | Business user | Identifies actual decision impact | | Internal audit | Tests classification controls | ### Permanent rule Classify the method and its use, not its technology label. "Spreadsheet", "algorithm" and "AI" do not determine model status by themselves. ### Never confuse [Model] and [Non-model tool] **Model** - uses assumptions and analytical techniques to transform inputs into estimates or decision-relevant outputs with model uncertainty. --- **Non-model tool** - performs deterministic processing without the model characteristics defined by the applicable framework, though it can still require strong controls. ### Permanent trap Treating "not a model" as "not risky". A material deterministic calculator can cause major loss even when legitimately outside the model inventory. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Definition / scope | Boundary / status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | SR 26-2: complex quantitative method using statistical/economic/financial theories on inputs for estimates. | Simple arithmetic/deterministic rules without those theories excluded. | | UK | SS1/23: quantitative methods using statistical/economic/financial/mathematical theories, techniques and assumptions. | Broader; material complex deterministic methods outside scope may still warrant MRM controls. | | EU | ECB Guide: CRR internal models. | No enterprise-wide definition. | | IN | Draft: broad input-processing-output test including internal/third-party/AI/ML systems. | Draft as at August 2026; issued 24 June 2026; consultation closed 24 July 2026. |

title: Model Risk as a Distinct Risk Type
one_screen: Model risk is the potential for adverse consequences from relying on a model whose design, data, implementation, limitations or use make its output unreliable for the decision being taken. It is distinct from the underlying risk being measured: the borrower can be unchanged while a credit model is wrong, and the market can be unchanged while a valuation model is wrong.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Object | What can go wrong | | :--- | :--- | | Underlying credit exposure | Borrower fails to pay | | Market position | Prices or rates move adversely | | Liquidity position | Cash cannot be raised when needed | | Model | The institution measures, predicts or acts on those risks incorrectly | A model can be technically sound yet still generate model risk if it is used outside its intended population, horizon or decision context. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model owner | Identifies and manages model-specific risk | | Business user | Understands limitations before consuming output | | MRM / validation | Independently challenges reliability and use | | Senior management | Oversees material model risk within appetite | ### Permanent rule Model risk belongs to the use of the representation, not to the underlying exposure itself. ### Never confuse [Model risk] and [Underlying financial risk] **Model risk** - risk that reliance on a model contributes to an adverse decision or outcome. --- **Underlying financial risk** - risk inherent in the exposure or activity being modelled, such as borrower default, market movement or funding stress. ### Permanent trap Explaining an unexpected loss entirely as "credit risk" or "market risk" without asking whether the model mismeasured the risk, was used outside scope or produced misleading outputs. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The cited frameworks differ in perimeter and prescription, but all treat model risk as a risk arising from model use rather than as another name for the risk the model measures.

title: Where Model Risk Comes From
one_screen: Model risk is rarely one defect called "bad modelling". It can enter through data, assumptions, methodology, implementation, use or environmental change, and the same bad output can require a completely different remedy depending on which source failed.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Source | Failure mode | Typical control response | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Data | Wrong, incomplete, biased, stale or unrepresentative inputs | Repair lineage, quality or sampling | | Assumptions | Simplifications cease to hold | Challenge, constrain or revise assumptions | | Methodology | Model form does not represent the problem adequately | Redesign or redevelop | | Implementation | Code, configuration or interface differs from approved design | Correct implementation and retest | | Use | Output is misinterpreted or applied outside intended scope | Restrict use, train users, reapprove | | Environment | Population, behaviour or relationships change | Monitor, recalibrate or redevelop | | Governance | Weak challenge allows known limitations to persist | Escalate, remediate, strengthen control | The categories can interact: Data shift → assumption no longer holds → calibration deteriorates → users apply stale output → losses increase Root-cause analysis therefore matters more than attaching a generic "model underperformance" label. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Developer / owner | Controls design, data and implementation risks | | Model user | Controls scope, interpretation and use risk | | MRM / validation | Challenges all sources and their interactions | | Internal audit | Assesses whether the control framework catches them | ### Permanent rule A performance symptom is not a root cause. Diagnose where the failure entered before choosing the remedy. ### Never confuse [Implementation error] and [Model limitation] **Implementation error** - the production system does not execute the approved model correctly. --- **Model limitation** - the approved model itself has a known boundary, approximation or uncertainty even when implemented exactly as designed. ### Permanent trap Responding to every poor result with recalibration. Recalibration may repair stale parameter levels; it does not fix corrupted data, bad code, conceptual misspecification or misuse. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Data, design, implementation, use and environmental change are universal sources even though regulators express them with different terminology.

title: The Regulatory Perimeter: US, UK, EU and India
one_screen: There is no single global legal perimeter for MRM. The US uses broad, tailored supervisory guidance; the PRA applies SS1/23 to specified firms but across their model types; the EU prudential regime focuses on approved internal models; and India's proposed 2026 framework is broader but remains draft as at August 2026.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Jurisdiction | Institution perimeter | Model perimeter | August 2026 status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | Most relevant above USD 30bn; possible relevance below where model risk is significant | Traditional quantitative and qualifying non-generative, non-agentic AI models | Live supervisory guidance | | UK | Specified PRA firms with internal model approval | SS1/23 principles across model and risk types in those firms | Live supervisory statement | | EU | CRR institutions using permitted internal approaches | Internal credit, market and counterparty credit risk models | Live prudential framework | | IN | Eleven proposed categories of RBI-regulated entities | All models, including third-party and AI/ML | Draft; consultation closed | Entity → applicable instrument → model population → control obligations A bank may voluntarily govern more models than the legal minimum. That policy choice does not make the regulatory perimeters identical. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Separate three questions: "Is this a model?", "Is this institution in scope?", and "Does this instrument apply?" A yes to one does not answer the others. ### Permanent trap Importing one jurisdiction's requirement into another and presenting it as universal. Scope and prescription genuinely differ here. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Scope | Status / delta | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | SR 26-2/OCC Bulletin 2026-13; most relevant above USD 30bn, potentially below where model risk is significant. | Issued 17 April 2026; replaced 2011 guidance; risk-based, non-prescriptive. | | UK | Specified PRA firms with internal-model approval; new permission gives 12 months to comply; principles extend beyond approved capital models. | Current SS1/23 effective 23 April 2026. | | EU | ECB Guide covers approved CRR internal models. | Revised 28 July 2025; supervisory CRR interpretation, not enterprise MRM code. | | IN | Proposed regulatory MRM framework. | Draft as at August 2026; issued 24 June 2026; comments closed 24 July 2026; placeholder circular number invalid. |

title: Model Inventory and Dependency Map
one_screen: The model inventory is the authoritative record of what models exist, where they are in the lifecycle, who owns and uses them, and which other systems or models they depend on. A mere list of names is insufficient: the control value comes from linking identity, status, use, lineage, dependencies and governance state.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Inventory field | Control question | | :--- | :--- | | Model ID/version | Exact governed object? | | Purpose/use | Which decision depends on it? | | Owner/user | Who is accountable/consumes output? | | Risk tier | Required control intensity? | | Status | Development, validation, active, restricted, inactive or retired? | | Validation/approval | Authorised, with what conditions? | | Upstream dependencies | What can contaminate it? | | Downstream consumers | What fails if it fails? | | Third-party status | External dependency? | | Limitations/issues | Known open weaknesses? | Model A data → Model B estimate → Model C decision output Dependency mapping links inventory rows into chains, exposing propagation when upstream failure contaminates downstream models. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model owner | Keeps model record accurate | | Business / technology | Confirms actual use and dependencies | | MRM function | Sets inventory standards and challenges completeness | | Internal audit | Tests completeness and reconciliation | ### Permanent rule One model has one governed identity, but it may have many uses, versions and dependencies. Inventory controls must preserve that distinction. ### Never confuse [Model inventory] and [Model repository] **Model inventory** - authoritative governance record showing models, status, ownership and control attributes. --- **Model repository** - storage location for code, documentation, artefacts or files; it may support the inventory but does not replace it. ### Permanent trap Keeping retired or restricted models invisible. Historical lineage matters for reproducing past decisions, understanding inherited outputs and managing transitions. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Inventory expectation | Scope / status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | Risk-based identification sufficient for individual and aggregate model-risk oversight; no fixed template. | 2026 guidance less prescriptive than predecessor. | | UK | SS1/23 Principle 1: identify models, maintain inventory, classify risk for proportionate controls. | Formal inventory expectation. | | EU | CRR/ECB governs prudential model scope, rating systems, changes and permissions. | No enterprise inventory mandate for every quantitative tool. | | IN | Proposed current inventory covering active, inactive, decommissioned, third-party and AI/ML models. | Draft as at August 2026; not final. |

title: Materiality and Risk Tiering
one_screen: Tiering converts model characteristics and business impact into proportional control intensity. The purpose is not to declare low-tier models harmless; it is to spend validation, approval, monitoring and governance effort where model failure can matter most while preserving a minimum control floor for every governed model.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Driver | What it captures | | :--- | :--- | | Inherent risk | Complexity, assumptions, input quality, data constraints | | Purpose | Importance of the decision or regulatory use | | Exposure | Scale of balances, customers, transactions or business affected | | Materiality | Significance of purpose plus exposure | | Consumer / operational impact | Harm beyond direct financial exposure | | Changeability | Dynamic behaviour or frequent updating | | Dependency | Whether other important models rely on it | A simple model can be high risk because its output affects a huge portfolio. A complex model can be lower materiality if it has narrow, non-critical use. Complexity and materiality therefore answer different questions. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Tiering scales controls; it never removes accountability. A lower tier means proportionate MRM, not exemption from all governance. ### Never confuse [Complexity] and [Materiality] **Complexity** - difficulty of understanding, estimating, implementing or challenging the model. --- **Materiality** - significance of the model's output to decisions and exposures. A model can be simple but highly material. ### Permanent trap Building a score that lets one benign factor cancel a critical one. A highly material model should not become "low risk" merely because its technique is simple. ### Jurisdiction variants #### US (Federal Reserve / OCC) SR 26-2 distinguishes inherent risk, model exposure and model purpose. Purpose together with exposure determines materiality; overall model risk reflects inherent risk in the context of materiality. Higher materiality warrants more rigorous oversight, while immaterial models may receive more limited controls. #### UK (PRA) SS1/23 expects firms to classify model risk and use proportionality so the level of MRM activity reflects the model's risk. The PRA does not require every firm to use the same numerical tiering scale. #### IN (RBI) As at August 2026, the RBI draft proposes risk-based tiering for all models, with materiality, complexity and other relevant factors considered collectively. The proposed tier drives validation, approval, monitoring, reporting and business-continuity intensity; high-risk models receive stronger governance. It remains draft.

title: Aggregate Model Risk and Risk Appetite
one_screen: Managing models one by one can miss the largest exposure: several individually acceptable models may rely on the same data, assumptions, vendor or economic relationship and fail together. Aggregate model risk therefore combines model-level risk with concentration and dependency, then compares that enterprise exposure with the institution's model risk appetite and tolerance.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Aggregation lens | Example question | | :--- | :--- | | Common data | How many models depend on the same customer master or market feed? | | Common methodology | Would one invalid assumption impair several models? | | Model chains | Does an upstream output feed many downstream decisions? | | Vendor concentration | Could one provider outage or defect affect many models? | | Business concentration | Are critical decisions clustered around a small model set? | | Technology concentration | Do several models share one platform or implementation layer? | Risk appetite states how much model risk the institution is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives. Tolerance converts that high-level appetite into actionable boundaries, escalation triggers or control expectations. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model owners | Report model-level risk and dependencies | | Enterprise MRM | Aggregates risk and identifies concentration | | Senior management | Operates within approved appetite | | Board / relevant committee | Oversees appetite and material breaches | ### Permanent rule Portfolio diversification of financial exposures does not guarantee diversification of model risk. Shared models, data and assumptions can create hidden common-mode failure. ### Never confuse [Model tier] and [Model risk appetite] **Model tier** - classification of one model used to scale its controls. --- **Model risk appetite** - enterprise statement of how much model risk the institution is prepared to accept and under what constraints. ### Permanent trap Adding model risk scores as though they were independent. Aggregation must recognise dependencies and correlated failure, not just arithmetic totals. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The exact appetite framework is institution-specific, but assessing model risk both individually and in aggregate and governing material exposures is a common MRM principle.

title: The Model Lifecycle and Its Control Gates
one_screen: A model lifecycle is not a project plan; it is a sequence of governed states in which evidence must be sufficient before the model can move forward. The key control idea is the gate: development does not grant use, validation does not grant approval, approval does not end monitoring, and change can reopen earlier gates.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Gate | Minimum decision | | :--- | :--- | | Development complete | Is the evidence pack sufficient for independent challenge? | | Validation complete | Is the model reliable enough for its intended use, with known limitations? | | Approval | Is residual model risk acceptable and use authorised? | | Deployment | Does production reproduce the approved model? | | Monitoring | Does evidence still support continued use? | | Change | Does the change reopen validation or approval? | | Retirement | Can use cease without breaking dependencies or records? | Lifecycle controls are recursive. A material change can return an active model to development, validation and approval rather than allowing an informal production patch. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model owner | Coordinates the model through lifecycle stages | | Developer | Produces development and change evidence | | Validation / MRM | Independently challenges relevant stages | | Approval authority | Authorises use and material changes | | Business user | Operates only within approved conditions | ### Permanent rule A lifecycle stage creates evidence; a gate creates authority. Evidence from one stage is not authority to skip the next. ### Never confuse [Validation] and [Approval] **Validation** - independent assessment of reliability, limitations and fitness for intended use. --- **Approval** - governance decision to accept residual risk and authorise specified use, possibly with conditions. ### Permanent trap Treating "live" as the final state. Production use begins a new control phase in which monitoring, issue management, change and eventual retirement remain governed. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The cited regimes use different language and degrees of prescription, but the lifecycle logic of development, challenge, approval, use, monitoring, change and exit is common.

title: Who Produces, Uses, Approves, Challenges and Audits
one_screen: Ownership is the load-bearing control in MRM because the same person should not create evidence, decide whether that evidence is convincing, accept the residual risk and audit the process. Effective governance separates production, consumption, approval, independent challenge and assurance while ensuring the challenger has expertise, standing and access to decision-makers.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Role | Produces | Approves | Consumes | Challenges | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Developer | Design, code, tests | No | Sometimes | No | | Owner / first line | Ownership, monitoring, remediation | Delegated non-validation decisions only | Yes | No | | Business user | Use evidence, feedback, overrides | Only if separately delegated | Yes | No | | Approval authority | Decision, conditions | Yes | May | Uses validation input | | MRM / validation | Validation evidence | No business approval | No routine first-line use | Yes | | Internal audit | Audit evidence | No | No | Framework effectiveness, not routine validation | Independence is functional: incentives, authority and escalation must permit genuine challenge. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule No role title creates independence by itself. Independence requires objective incentives, sufficient expertise, organisational standing and authority to escalate or effect change. ### Never confuse [Independent validation] and [Internal audit] **Independent validation** - challenges specific model reliability, limitations and use as part of normal MRM. --- **Internal audit** - independently assesses whether the MRM framework, policies and controls are designed and operating effectively; it does not ordinarily duplicate development or validation. ### Permanent trap Calling the second line "the model owner". The owner remains accountable for the model; independent challenge must not absorb first-line responsibility merely because it can block or condition use. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Accountability | Independence / status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | Clear accountability; no prescribed organisation. | Objective effective challenge with independence, standing and influence; conflicts managed. | | UK | Board/senior-management accountability; appropriate SMF holder(s) own overall MRM. | Independent validation alongside accountable management. | | IN | Proposed three lines: owners; independent MRM/validation; internal audit, plus Board/RMCB duties. | Draft as at August 2026; not final. |

title: Purpose, Intended Use and Limitations
one_screen: Development begins by fixing the decision the model is supposed to support, the population and conditions it covers, and the limitations users must respect. Without that mandate, developers cannot choose evidence coherently and validators cannot decide whether "good performance" is relevant to the actual use.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Development mandate | Question | | :--- | :--- | | Objective | What problem is the model solving? | | Output | What exactly will it estimate, rank, classify or optimise? | | Population | For which customers, products, markets or processes? | | Horizon | Over what time period is the output meaningful? | | Intended use | Which decisions may consume the output? | | Prohibited use | Where must it not be used without further analysis? | | Performance criteria | What evidence will count as adequate? | | Limitations | Which assumptions, data gaps or boundary conditions remain? | | Alternatives | What happens if the model is unavailable or unsuitable? | Purpose → data choice → methodology → testing → validation → use conditions A one-line reminder is enough where the model produces familiar risk parameters: PD, LGD and EAD are model outputs used in credit-risk contexts; their substantive estimation belongs elsewhere. MRM asks whether the model's stated purpose and permitted use match the evidence. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Business user | Defines decision context and operational need | | Model owner | Owns documented purpose and use boundaries | | Developer | Designs consistently with that mandate | | Validation | Challenges whether mandate and evidence align | ### Permanent rule A model is fit for a use, not "fit" in the abstract. Change the use materially and the original evidence may no longer support the decision. ### Never confuse [Limitation] and [Defect] **Limitation** - known boundary or uncertainty inherent in the model that may be acceptable with controls. --- **Defect** - error or failure that makes the model inconsistent with its approved design or required standard. ### Permanent trap Writing broad purposes such as "risk management". Vague mandates make almost any data, method or later use appear defensible and prevent meaningful challenge. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Clear purpose, intended use and understanding of limitations are universal development and use principles; regulators differ mainly in scope and prescription, not in this mechanism.

title: Data Lineage and Fitness for Use
one_screen: Model data is not sound merely because it is clean. It must be traceable from source to model, correctly transformed, sufficiently complete, representative of the intended use and governed consistently between development and production; a perfectly coded model trained or run on unsuitable data remains unreliable.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism At every step ask: complete? accurate? timely? representative? reproducible? controlled? | Data property | Validation question | | :--- | :--- | | Provenance | Where did the field originate? | | Lineage | What transformations occurred before use? | | Accuracy | Does the value represent what the model assumes it represents? | | Completeness | Are missing observations understood and treated consistently? | | Representativeness | Does development evidence reflect the intended population and conditions? | | Stability | Has the distribution or meaning changed? | | Consistency | Do development and production definitions match? | | Access / retention | Can the evidence be reproduced and challenged later? | Synthetic data does not remove these questions; it adds questions about generation logic, realism and whether synthetic patterns distort the relationship the model is meant to learn. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Data owner | Authoritative definitions and quality controls | | Developer | Documents selection, transformations and exclusions | | Model owner | Ensures production feed remains fit for use | | Validation | Independently tests lineage, relevance and representativeness | ### Permanent rule Data quality is purpose-dependent. The same dataset can be adequate for one model and inadequate for another because target population, horizon or required precision differ. ### Never confuse [Data accuracy] and [Data representativeness] **Data accuracy** - recorded values correctly reflect the underlying observations. --- **Data representativeness** - the observations collectively reflect the population and conditions for which the model will be used. ### Permanent trap Treating a successful data-quality dashboard as proof of model-data suitability. Fields can be complete and internally consistent while the sample is stale, selected or irrelevant to the intended use. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Data governance vocabulary varies, but traceability, quality, relevance and consistency between development and use are common model-development and validation expectations.

title: Method, Assumptions and Complexity
one_screen: Method selection is a governed judgement about whether the model structure, assumptions and complexity are appropriate for the stated purpose and available data. MRM does not own the derivation of statistical methods; it owns the evidence that the chosen method is defensible, its assumptions are visible, and added complexity earns its place.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Question | Evidence expected | | :--- | :--- | | Why this method? | Link to purpose, output and decision need | | What assumptions matter? | Explicit assumptions and conditions under which they fail | | What alternatives were considered? | Comparison sufficient to show selection was reasoned | | What does complexity add? | Better performance, stability, flexibility or decision usefulness | | What does complexity cost? | Explainability, data dependence, implementation and validation burden | | Where is judgement embedded? | Variable choices, segmentation, constraints, overrides or expert assumptions | A more complex model is not inherently superior. Complexity increases the number of ways assumptions, interactions, implementation and user understanding can fail. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Developer | Selects and documents method and assumptions | | Model owner | Accepts design rationale for intended use | | Business user | Provides practical context and challenges implausible behaviour | | Validation | Independently challenges conceptual soundness | ### Permanent rule Complexity must be justified by useful model capability, not by technical sophistication alone. ### Never confuse [Assumption] and [Parameter] **Assumption** - proposition or simplification the model relies on, such as stability of a relationship or suitability of a data treatment. --- **Parameter** - estimated or set quantity within the chosen model structure. Updating a parameter does not necessarily repair a broken assumption. ### Permanent trap Using strong historical fit as proof of conceptual soundness. A misspecified or over-complex model can fit development data very well while relying on unstable or spurious relationships. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The technical methods vary by model, but regulators consistently expect methodology, assumptions and judgement to be documented, challenged and proportionate to use and materiality.

title: Implementation, Versioning and Reproducibility
one_screen: A validated methodology is useless if production executes something different. Implementation control proves that approved logic, data transformations, parameters, dependencies and configuration are faithfully reproduced, while versioning and reproducibility make it possible to determine exactly which model generated a past output.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Control | What it prevents | | :--- | :--- | | Source control | Undocumented code changes | | Unique version | Ambiguity about which model was used | | Peer / independent code review | Logic and implementation errors | | Test cases | Silent calculation defects | | Development-production reconciliation | Different transformations or parameters | | Dependency pinning | Uncontrolled library or service changes | | Release approval | Unauthorised production updates | | Execution logs | Inability to reconstruct model behaviour | Reproducibility means that with the governed model version, relevant inputs and environment, the institution can reconstruct or adequately evidence how the output was produced. For stochastic models, reproducibility may require seeds, configuration and retained run metadata rather than identical output in every context. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Developer | Implements and unit-tests approved logic | | Technology / MLOps | Controls environments, release and dependencies | | Model owner | Ensures governed version matches authorised use | | Validation | Tests implementation consistency and reproducibility | ### Permanent rule A model version is part of the model identity. Change code, parameters, transformations or material configuration and the governance question is whether you still have the approved model. ### Never confuse [Methodology validation] and [Implementation verification] **Methodology validation** - asks whether the model concept and assumptions are appropriate. --- **Implementation verification** - asks whether the executable system faithfully performs that approved concept. ### Permanent trap Validating a development notebook and assuming production is identical. Differences in code, data transformation, libraries, interfaces or configuration can create a new failure mode after technical validation. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Implementation assurance and reproducibility are general controls; exact technology standards vary by institution rather than by the core MRM principle.

title: Developer Testing and the Pre-Validation Evidence Pack
one_screen: Developer testing is first-line evidence that the model behaves as intended before independent validation begins. It should expose weaknesses rather than manufacture a pass: the pre-validation pack must show what was tested, what failed, what changed, what remains limited and why the developer still believes the model is fit to be challenged for its intended use.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Evidence area | Developer question | | :--- | :--- | | Data | Are quality, selection and transformations tested? | | Logic | Does implementation match the specification? | | Sensitivity | Do outputs move plausibly when important inputs or assumptions move? | | Robustness | Does performance depend excessively on one sample or choice? | | Generalisation | Does evidence hold outside the fitting sample where appropriate? | | Alternatives | Were reasonable competing assumptions or methods considered? | | Edge cases | What happens under unusual, missing or extreme inputs? | | Limitations | What known weakness remains after development? | Out-of-sample and out-of-time tests may be useful, but this atom does not teach their statistics. The point is governance: development evidence must be relevant to the model's stated purpose and difficult enough to reveal failure. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Developer | Designs, executes and documents testing | | Model owner | Confirms evidence pack is complete | | Business user | Provides practical challenge and unusual-use cases | | Validation | Reviews and independently extends the testing where needed | ### Permanent rule Developer testing is necessary evidence, but it is not independent validation. The person proving the model was built carefully is not the final challenger of that proof. ### Never confuse [Developer testing] and [Independent validation] **Developer testing** - first-line testing used to design, debug and evidence the candidate model. --- **Independent validation** - objective challenge of the model and the sufficiency of the developer's evidence, supplemented by independent analysis where warranted. ### Permanent trap Removing failed tests from the final pack. A documented failure and reasoned remediation is evidence of control; a polished record that hides development weaknesses deprives validators of the most informative evidence. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The 2026 US guidance expressly recognises model testing as a core development activity and scales rigor to complexity and materiality; the underlying first-line versus independent-challenge distinction is universal.

title: Independent Validation: Mandate, Independence and Timing
one_screen: Independent validation asks whether the model is reliable enough for its intended use, what limitations remain, and what controls or corrective actions are required. Independence is substantive, not ceremonial: validators need technical competence, objective incentives, access to evidence and organisational standing to challenge the model owner effectively.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Independence dimension | What good looks like | | :--- | :--- | | Organisational | Validation is not controlled by model development or use | | Incentives | Validator is not rewarded for getting the model approved | | Expertise | Validator can understand and challenge the model's methods | | Access | Validator can obtain data, code, documentation and users | | Standing | Findings can reach decision-makers and delay or restrict use | | Scope | Validation can extend testing when developer evidence is weak | Timing should be risk-based. First-use validation is the normal control point; material changes, emerging weaknesses or changing conditions can trigger renewed validation. A fixed calendar alone is insufficient because a stable low-risk model and a rapidly changing material model should not receive identical attention. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Validation must be able to reach an unfavourable conclusion without organisational pressure to approve the model. ### Never confuse [Validation independence] and [Physical separation] **Validation independence** - sufficient objectivity, expertise, authority and freedom from conflicting incentives to challenge the model. --- **Physical separation** - different desks, teams or reporting lines. It may support independence but does not guarantee it. ### Permanent trap Using an annual validation calendar as proof of control. Frequency should respond to purpose, materiality, methodology, model change, data limitations and emerging evidence. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Timing / frequency | Independence / status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | Scales with use, materiality, methodology, change, data limits and constraints. | Usually pre-use; urgent early use needs limits, stakeholder communication and heightened monitoring. | | UK | Proportionate to model risk. | Principle 4: independent validation, effective challenge, separation from development/use. | | EU | Ongoing assessment commensurate with prudential-model risk. | Independent validation embedded in CRR/ECB governance. | | IN | Proposed pre/post-deployment, after modifications/triggers and periodically. | All models; draft as at August 2026, not final. |

title: The Validation Work Programme
one_screen: A validation work programme turns "independent challenge" into a reproducible examination of the whole model. It asks whether the concept is sound, the data are fit, implementation matches design, performance evidence is persuasive, limitations are understood and actual use stays inside the model's supported boundaries.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Workstream | Validator's question | | :--- | :--- | | Purpose and use | Is the model solving the stated problem and being judged against the right criteria? | | Conceptual soundness | Are methodology, assumptions and judgement defensible? | | Data | Are sources, transformations and populations fit for use? | | Implementation | Does executable production logic match approved design? | | Development evidence | Were tests sufficiently demanding and transparent? | | Outcomes | Does realised evidence support ranking, levels and predictions? | | Stability | Have population or relationships moved? | | Benchmarking | Does an independent comparator reveal weakness? | | Limitations | Are weaknesses explicit, bounded and controlled? | | Use | Are users operating within approved scope? | Validation is not a checklist where strong performance on one dimension cancels a fundamental failure on another. High discrimination, for example, cannot make corrupted data or unauthorised use acceptable. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Validation lead | Sets risk-based scope and conclusion | | Specialist validators | Perform technical and data challenge | | Model owner | Supplies complete evidence and responds to challenge | | Business user | Explains actual use and limitations in practice | ### Permanent rule Validation evaluates the model as a used decision system, not only as a mathematical object. ### Never confuse [Validation scope] and [Validation checklist] **Validation scope** - risk-based set of questions and tests needed to support a conclusion on the specific model. --- **Validation checklist** - control aid that can promote consistency but cannot decide which evidence is materially important. ### Permanent trap Declaring a model valid because every standard template field is complete. Documentation completeness is evidence of governance, not proof that the model is conceptually or empirically reliable. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The exact depth varies with model type and materiality, but conceptual soundness, data, implementation, performance, limitations and use are common dimensions of robust validation.

title: Outcomes Analysis: Discrimination, Calibration and Backtesting
one_screen: Outcomes analysis asks whether model outputs correspond to real-world outcomes in the way the model's purpose requires. Discrimination tests ranking, calibration tests level accuracy, and backtesting compares prior predictions with realised outcomes; none of them alone establishes that the entire model is sound.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Instrument | Question it answers | Breach means | It cannot prove | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | AUC / Gini / KS | Does the model separate or rank outcomes effectively? | Ranking power has weakened or is inadequate for use | Probability levels are accurate | | Calibration test / plot | Do predicted levels align with observed levels? | Systematic over- or under-prediction may exist | Cases are ranked well | | Backtesting | Did prior forecasts correspond to realised outcomes over the test period? | Forecast behaviour differs from expectation | Future validity under changed conditions | Thresholds should be set for the model and use, not copied as universal regulatory numbers. Statistical significance also does not automatically equal economic significance; sample size, data quality and consequence matter. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Ranking and level accuracy are different properties. A model can rank cases correctly while consistently predicting the wrong absolute level. ### Never confuse [Discrimination] and [Calibration] **Discrimination** - ability to order observations so relatively higher-risk cases receive relatively higher-risk model outputs. --- **Calibration** - alignment between predicted levels and observed outcome frequencies or values. ### Permanent trap Teaching a fixed AUC, KS or calibration threshold as a universal pass mark. Thresholds are model- and use-specific governance choices unless a particular applicable rule states otherwise. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Regulators differ in model scope and supervisory detail, but discrimination, calibration and backtesting are technical validation instruments; the mathematics does not change by jurisdiction.

title: Stability, Benchmarking and Challenger Models
one_screen: Stability analysis asks whether the population or model relationships have moved; benchmarking asks whether an independent reference gives a materially different view. These controls catch weaknesses that a model's own historical performance can miss: a stable model can be consistently wrong, and a challenger can reveal a better explanation without automatically becoming the production model.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Instrument | Core question | Signal | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | PSI | Has a score or variable distribution shifted between reference and current populations? | Population drift | | CSI | Has the distribution of a characteristic shifted? | Feature-level drift | | Benchmark | Does an independent method, external reference or simpler estimate produce materially different results? | Possible bias, misspecification or hidden assumption | | Challenger | Can an alternative model explain or predict the target materially better or more robustly? | Incumbent may be stale or unnecessarily complex | Reference population → current population → stability measure → investigate shift PSI and CSI are signals, not verdicts. A large distribution shift can arise from genuine business mix changes, economic movement or data defects. Conversely, low PSI does not prove correctness: the population can remain stable while the model is structurally biased or poorly calibrated. A challenger is evidence, not a replacement. Replacement requires its own development, validation, approval and implementation controls. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Stability asks "has it moved?", not "is it right?". Benchmarking asks "what does another credible lens say?", not "which model wins one metric?". ### Never confuse [Benchmark] and [Challenger] **Benchmark** - independent reference used to test reasonableness, which may be simpler, external or non-production. --- **Challenger** - alternative model deliberately developed to compete with or test the incumbent on relevant performance and robustness dimensions. ### Permanent trap Using the common PSI rules of thumb as automatic regulatory limits. Bin design, sample size, business context and model purpose affect interpretation; a breach should trigger investigation, not mechanical model failure. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Stability statistics and independent comparators are validation instruments; there is no jurisdiction-specific mathematics and no universal supervisory PSI threshold to manufacture.

title: Validation Findings and Issue Disposition
one_screen: Validation evidence must end in a decision-useful opinion, not a pile of tests. Findings translate observed weaknesses into severity, required action, ownership and closure evidence; the validation opinion then states whether the model is fit for intended use, fit only with limitations or not fit, without pretending that validation itself grants approval.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Finding field | What it must answer | | :--- | :--- | | Observation | What is wrong or uncertain? | | Consequence | Which output, use or decision can be affected? | | Severity | How material is the resulting model risk? | | Root cause | Data, method, implementation, use or governance? | | Action | What must change? | | Interim control | How is risk contained before permanent fix? | | Owner / due date | Who is accountable and by when? | | Closure evidence | What proves the issue is actually resolved? | A practical opinion scale can distinguish: - Fit for intended use. - Fit subject to defined limitations, controls or remediation. - Not fit for intended use. The labels are institution-specific; the essential point is that the conclusion reflects residual risk, not merely the number of findings. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Validator | Owns finding and independent closure assessment | | Model owner | Owns remediation | | Business user | Implements interim use restrictions | | Governance body | Oversees overdue or material issues | ### Permanent rule The model owner fixes the problem; the independent challenger decides whether evidence supports closing the finding. ### Never confuse [Validation opinion] and [Model approval] **Validation opinion** - independent conclusion on reliability, limitations and conditions. --- **Model approval** - governance decision to authorise use and accept residual risk after considering validation and business context. ### Permanent trap Closing findings because the due date arrived or management accepted the risk. Risk acceptance can permit continued use; it does not prove the technical weakness disappeared. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Finding taxonomies differ across institutions, but translating validation weaknesses into accountable remediation and controlled closure is a universal governance mechanism.

title: Approval and Conditions of Use
one_screen: Approval is the governance act that accepts or rejects residual model risk for a defined use after considering validation, limitations and business need. It can be unconditional, conditional or refused; a conditional approval is a controlled risk decision with explicit restrictions and expiry or remediation, not a way to bypass unresolved validation.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Approval record | Required content | | :--- | :--- | | Model / version | Exact object authorised | | Intended use | Permitted decision and population | | Validation status | Findings and limitations considered | | Conditions | Limits, overlays, monitoring or remediation | | Exceptions | Rationale and compensating controls | | Authority | Person or committee with delegated power | | Duration | Expiry or review point where conditional | | Escalation | What triggers restriction or withdrawal | Urgent need may justify controlled exceptional use in some frameworks, but the logic remains the same: uncertainty is made explicit and compensated by stronger controls rather than silently ignored. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Approval authorises a specific model version for a specific use under stated conditions. It is not a permanent certificate of general correctness. ### Never confuse [Conditional approval] and [Validation waiver] **Conditional approval** - governance accepts limited residual risk subject to explicit restrictions, remediation or enhanced monitoring. --- **Validation waiver** - absence of required independent challenge. These are not equivalent; conditional use should not erase the need for validation where the framework requires it. ### Permanent trap Treating executive urgency as evidence that model risk is acceptable. Urgency affects the risk decision and controls; it does not improve model reliability. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Approval / use | Exception / status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | Validation generally before first use. | Urgent early use may proceed with limits, stakeholder awareness and closer monitoring. | | UK | Proportionate governance; clear approval/escalation. | Validation and senior accountability remain distinct. | | EU | Internal approval plus CRR controls. | Use/material changes may need supervisory permission/notification. | | IN | Draft: formal approval, documented exceptions, stronger high-risk approval including RMCB. | Draft as at August 2026; not binding. |

title: Deployment, Use and Overrides
one_screen: A model is not controlled merely because the approved code reaches production. Deployment must reproduce the approved model, users must understand what the output means and where it is limited, and manual overrides must be visible enough to distinguish healthy expert judgement from systematic evidence that the model or its use is failing.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Use control | Question | | :--- | :--- | | Production reconciliation | Does live output match the approved implementation? | | Access | Who can run or alter the model? | | User guidance | Do users understand output, assumptions and limitations? | | Scope controls | Can prohibited uses be prevented or detected? | | Override authority | Who can depart from model output? | | Reason codes | Why was the override made? | | Outcome tracking | Did overrides improve or worsen decisions? | | Usage evidence | Is the model actually used where governance assumes it is? | Overrides are not inherently bad. Expert judgement can correct a known model limitation or incorporate information unavailable to the model. Risk rises when overrides are frequent, one-directional, poorly documented or concentrated by user or segment. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Technology | Deploys the approved version and protects release controls | | Business user | Uses output within scope and documents overrides | | Model owner | Monitors usage and override patterns | | MRM / validation | Challenges misuse and systematic override behaviour | ### Permanent rule A manual override changes the decision, not the model. If repeated overrides reveal structural weakness, fix or restrict the model rather than normalising permanent manual correction. ### Never confuse [Override] and [Model adjustment] **Override** - case-specific human decision that departs from model output. --- **Model adjustment** - systematic change to model output, logic or post-model treatment applied across defined cases and governed as model change or mitigation. ### Permanent trap Monitoring only override frequency. Ten justified overrides can be healthier than two undocumented ones; direction, reason, user concentration and realised outcome matter. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The use-control mechanism is universal even though particular sectors or models may have separate use-test or approval requirements.

title: Ongoing Monitoring, Thresholds and Escalation
one_screen: Ongoing monitoring asks whether a live model is still performing as expected as products, exposures, customers, data and market conditions change. A monitoring framework is complete only when each signal has an owner, threshold, investigation path and escalation action; a metric dashboard without decisions attached is observation, not control.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Monitoring lens | Typical evidence | What a breach asks | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Outcomes | Realised versus predicted results | Has performance deteriorated? | | Discrimination / calibration | Relevant performance instruments | Is ranking or level accuracy weakening? | | Stability | Population and characteristic shifts | Has the model environment moved? | | Data | Quality, missingness, lineage changes | Is the input process still fit? | | Overrides / use | Frequency, direction and reason | Are users compensating for weakness or misusing output? | | Limitations | Known constraints and assumptions | Has a known limitation become more material? | | Operations | Failures, latency, dependencies | Is implementation or service reliability changing? | Thresholds can be hard limits, tolerance bands or qualitative triggers. They should be tied to the model's intended use and consequence, with escalation stronger when breaches are persistent, material or clustered across several indicators. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model owner | Runs or coordinates monitoring and investigates breaches | | Business user | Reports use issues and decision impacts | | MRM / validation | Challenges thresholds, trends and remediation | | Governance body | Receives material or overdue escalations | ### Permanent rule A threshold breach is a trigger for governed investigation, not an automatic diagnosis of model failure. ### Never confuse [Monitoring] and [Validation] **Monitoring** - recurring first-line and governance surveillance of live performance, data, use and environment. --- **Validation** - independent assessment of reliability and limitations, which can use monitoring evidence but is not replaced by it. ### Permanent trap Resetting thresholds after repeated breaches merely to restore a green dashboard. Threshold changes themselves require rationale because they alter the institution's definition of acceptable model behaviour. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The 2026 US guidance explicitly scales monitoring frequency and scope to model nature, new data, modelling approaches and materiality; that risk-based principle is consistent with sound MRM elsewhere.

title: Model Change: Adjustment, Recalibration or Redevelopment
one_screen: Model change begins with classification because different interventions solve different problems and reopen different controls. An overlay or adjustment can mitigate a known weakness, recalibration updates levels within an existing structure, and redevelopment changes the model fundamentally; none should become an undocumented production patch.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Intervention | What changes | Appropriate when | Control question | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Correction | Code, data mapping or implementation | Approved design was implemented wrongly | Was the defect removed and retested? | | Overlay / adjustment | Output outside the core model | Temporary limitation needs mitigation | Is scope and removal criterion controlled? | | Recalibration | Parameters or level alignment | Structure remains sound but levels drifted | Does evidence support retaining the model form? | | Redevelopment | Variables, architecture, method or core assumptions | Structural weakness or new purpose makes the old model inadequate | Is this effectively a new model? | Change materiality follows effect on behaviour, assumptions, data, use, regulatory status and dependencies, not the size of the code change. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model owner / developer | Proposes change and materiality | | MRM / validation | Challenges classification and validates as required | | Approval authority | Approves material changes or exceptions | | Technology | Releases authorised versions only | ### Permanent rule A one-line parameter or transformation change can materially alter outputs. Technical size is not model-risk size. ### Never confuse [Recalibration] and [Redevelopment] **Recalibration** - updates parameters or level alignment while preserving the essential structure and intended use. --- **Redevelopment** - materially changes structure, drivers, architecture or assumptions and therefore creates substantially new development evidence. ### Permanent trap Keeping an overlay indefinitely because it is easier than fixing the model. Temporary mitigation needs an owner, rationale, review point and exit criterion. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Change rule | Delta / status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | Deviation can trigger adjustment/recalibration/redevelopment; validation follows change scope/frequency. | No fixed schedule. | | UK | Proportionate governance/validation/mitigants. | SS1/23 applies. | | EU | Internal control + CRR/ECB change process. | Approval/notification may apply. | | IN | Draft: post-change/trigger validation + formal approval. | Draft as at August 2026. |

title: Retirement and Decommissioning
one_screen: Retirement is a controlled lifecycle transition, not deletion. Before a model leaves service, the institution must understand why it is being retired, what replaces it, which downstream processes depend on it, how historical decisions remain reproducible and what records must be retained.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Retirement trigger → dependency/use assessment → replacement/fallback → approval → production access removed → inventory updated → evidence archived | Question | Required answer | | :--- | :--- | | Why retire? | Obsolescence, replacement, poor performance, business exit or regulatory change | | Dependencies? | Models, reports, decisions, interfaces and users | | Replacement? | New model, manual process, vendor service or none | | Reproducibility? | Historical outputs, decisions and regulatory evidence | | Residual access? | Read-only archive versus production execution | | Open issues? | Transfer to replacement or close with use | | Closure owner? | Model owner plus technology/governance functions | Exit is incomplete while hidden spreadsheets, APIs or downstream processes still call the model; that leaves an ownerless orphan model. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model owner | Initiates and documents decommissioning | | Business / technology | Removes use and manages dependencies | | MRM function | Challenges retirement completeness | | Records / governance | Preserves required evidence | ### Permanent rule Retired means no longer used for live decisions; it does not mean its evidence can immediately disappear. ### Never confuse [Retirement] and [Deletion] **Retirement** - governed removal from active use while preserving required lineage, records and historical reproducibility. --- **Deletion** - destruction of an artefact. It may be prohibited by retention requirements and is not itself a lifecycle process. ### Permanent trap Decommissioning an upstream model without tracing downstream consumers. A successful technical shutdown can still break reports, challenger processes or other models that depended on its output. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Exit expectation | Retention / status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | Principles-based decommissioning. | No universal retention period; legal, recordkeeping and risk needs govern. | | UK | Inventory/lifecycle governance through exit. | No Indian-style ten-year rule. | | EU | Internal retirement plus CRR/ECB processes where prudential models are replaced. | Permissions/replacement arrangements may apply. | | IN | Draft keeps decommissioned models in inventory at least ten years. | Proposed only; not in force as at August 2026. |

title: Third-Party and Vendor Models
one_screen: Buying a model changes access and dependency, not accountability. The institution still needs enough understanding, evidence and contractual rights to judge suitability for its own use, validate it proportionately, monitor it, control vendor changes and exit safely if the product or provider fails.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Need → due diligence → method/data/limits understood → access/change rights → independent validation → approval → monitoring/change control → continuity/exit | Control | Core question | | :--- | :--- | | Provider | Can it support/govern the product? | | Transparency | Can the bank challenge suitability? | | Data | Relevant to bank population/use? | | Validation access | Enough evidence for independent challenge? | | Change notice | Will method/data/version changes be known? | | Outcomes | Can bank experience monitor performance? | | Concentration | Critical reliance on vendor/platform? | | Continuity/exit | Can the bank operate, replace or migrate? | Vendor certification or external assurance is evidence, not a substitute for the bank's own fitness-for-use judgement. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Business / model owner | Remains accountable for use and outcomes | | Procurement / third-party risk | Supports due diligence and contracts | | Vendor | Supplies agreed documentation and change information | | MRM / validation | Independently challenges institution-specific use | ### Permanent rule Outsourcing model development does not outsource model risk ownership. ### Never confuse [Vendor due diligence] and [Model validation] **Vendor due diligence** - assesses provider capability, resilience, governance and contractual suitability. --- **Model validation** - assesses whether the model is reliable and appropriate for the institution's intended use. ### Permanent trap Accepting "proprietary" as a complete answer to validation questions. Where full internals cannot be disclosed, alternative evidence and stronger controls must still support a defensible use decision. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Accountability | Control / status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | Dedicated vendor/third-party section; bank retains oversight. | May use vendor evidence, but must understand product and assess own-use performance. | | UK | In-scope vendor/external models remain under SS1/23. | Outsourcing does not transfer MRM responsibility. | | EU | Third-party components do not transfer prudential-model responsibility. | Institution remains responsible under CRR/ECB expectations. | | IN | Draft expressly covers third-party models; regulated entity remains accountable. | Proposed due diligence, validation documentation/access, continuity and exit; draft as at August 2026. |

title: AI/ML Governance: Complexity, Explainability and Human Control
one_screen: AI/ML models remain models where the applicable framework puts them in scope, but opacity, dynamic behaviour and automation can intensify familiar MRM problems. Governance asks whether complexity is justified, decisions can be explained, humans retain control, and the institution can stop or fall back safely.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | AI/ML issue | Control question | | :--- | :--- | | Complexity | What decision benefit justifies harder challenge? | | Explainability | Can users and validators understand important drivers and limitations? | | Training data | Is provenance, quality and representativeness traceable? | | Bias / fairness | Are material outcome differences identified and governed? | | Automation | Can users recognise when output should not be accepted automatically? | | Human oversight | Who can review, override, suspend or escalate? | | Dynamic updating | Can behaviour change without an ordinary release event? | | Fallback | What happens if the model is unavailable or unsafe? | Explainability is purpose-dependent: developers, decision users and validators need different kinds of explanation. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Higher predictive performance does not cancel governability. If a material model cannot be understood, challenged, controlled or stopped, performance alone is insufficient. ### Never confuse [Explainability] and [Accuracy] **Explainability** - ability to communicate relevant factors, behaviour or reasons at the level needed by the use and audience. --- **Accuracy** - degree to which outputs correspond to targets or realised outcomes. A model can be accurate yet insufficiently explainable. ### Permanent trap Adding a post-hoc explanation tool and treating the model as fully understood. Explanation methods are analytical tools with their own faithfulness and limitations. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | AI/ML scope | Governance / status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | SR 26-2: qualifying non-generative/non-agentic AI; generative/agentic excluded. | Broader governance remains needed outside guidance; as at August 2026. | | UK | SS1/23: in-scope AI/ML. | Manage AI/ML model risk. | | EU | ECB Guide 28-Jul-2025: prudential ML; AI Act: specified natural-person creditworthiness/credit-scoring can be Annex III high-risk. | Both may apply; Act generally applies 2-Aug-2026 subject to staged provisions. | | IN | Draft: explainability/human-oversight/customer-disclosure-assistance/dynamic-update/override-suspend-deactivate controls. | Draft as at August 2026; consultation closed 24 July 2026; not final. |

title: AI/ML Validation: Generalisation, Drift and Robustness
one_screen: AI/ML validation extends ordinary model challenge. It retains purpose, data, conceptual soundness, outcomes and use, while adding emphasis on generalisation, overfitting, drift, robustness, subgroup behaviour, explainability and post-deployment change.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Validation lens | Validator asks | | :--- | :--- | | Generalisation | Does performance persist outside development data and familiar conditions? | | Overfitting | Has the model learned noise rather than durable relationships? | | Drift | Are inputs, outputs or relationships changing after deployment? | | Robustness | Do small plausible changes cause unstable outputs? | | Subgroup performance | Are weaknesses concentrated in relevant populations? | | Explainability | Are explanations sufficiently faithful and stable for their purpose? | | Dynamic behaviour | Can retraining or automatic updates alter the governed model? | | Stress / challenge testing | What happens under unusual or deliberately difficult inputs? | Red-teaming intentionally seeks harmful, unstable or policy-breaking behaviour under realistic risk scenarios. It complements ordinary validation. This pack owns the validator's use of evidence, not ML mathematics or test derivation. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Average accuracy is weak evidence when failure concentrates in edge cases, subgroups or changed environments. Validation must look for where the model breaks. ### Never confuse [Drift] and [Overfitting] **Drift** - live data or the relationship between inputs and outcomes changes after development. --- **Overfitting** - the model learned development-specific noise or patterns that fail to generalise even without genuine external change. ### Permanent trap Validating the explanation method but not the model behaviour it claims to explain. A plausible explanation can still be unstable, incomplete or unfaithful. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Scope | Delta/status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | SR 26-2: qualifying non-generative/non-agentic AI. | Generative/agentic excluded as at August 2026. | | UK | SS1/23: in-scope AI/ML. | Independent-validation/MRM applies. | | EU | ECB-Guide-28-Jul-2025: prudential ML; AI-Act: high-risk AI. | Generally applies 2-Aug-2026 subject to transition. | | IN | Draft AI/ML validation. | Explainability/overfitting/bias/output-variability/data-risk/relevant-red-teaming/dynamic-updates proposed as at August 2026. |

title: Lending Populations, Samples and Sampling Frames
one_screen: A credit model never learns from "all borrowers". It learns from a sampling frame created by a lender's products, approval rules, geography, data retention and observation period, so the first statistical question is whether the development sample represents the lending population where the model will be used.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Layer | Credit meaning | Failure mode | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Target population | Borrowers or facilities about which an inference is required | Defined too broadly to match actual deployment | | Sampling frame | Cases the bank could observe and retrieve | Excludes rejects, closed accounts, acquired books or older vintages | | Realised sample | Records surviving filters, joins and cleaning | Further loss through missing data or eligibility rules | | Deployment population | Cases scored after implementation | Mix shifts away from development data | Sampling error is random variation from observing only part of the frame. Sampling bias is systematic distortion because some kinds of borrowers are more or less likely to appear. More data reduces sampling error but does not repair a biased frame. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Precision cannot rescue representativeness. A precisely estimated quantity from the wrong lending population is still the wrong quantity. ### Never confuse [Sampling error] and [Sampling bias] **Sampling error** - random difference caused by observing a finite sample. --- **Sampling bias** - systematic difference caused by who can enter or remain in the sample. ### Permanent trap Treating the bank's available dataset as the population. Availability is a property of the data estate, not proof that the observed borrowers represent the cases the model will score. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Population, sampling-frame and bias concepts are mathematical and do not change by regulator.

title: Credit Labels, Observation Windows and Censoring
one_screen: A binary credit label is not created merely by writing default = 1. The analyst must define an observation start, a performance horizon and what happens to accounts whose outcome is not fully observable; otherwise identical borrowers can receive different labels only because one has been watched longer.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism CR owns default as a governed credit status. QNT owns the statistical construction of an analyzable outcome from that status across time. | Case at observation date | Status after horizon | Statistical treatment | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Default occurs within full horizon | Event observed | Label 1 | | Full horizon completes without default | Non-event observed | Label 0 | | Account has not yet completed horizon | Outcome incomplete | Right-censored or excluded under a governed rule | | Account exits for a competing reason | Outcome path interrupted | Requires explicit competing-risk or censoring treatment | ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule A non-default label requires enough observation time to know that default did not occur inside the defined horizon. ### Never confuse [Non-default] and [Censored] **Non-default** - the required performance window completed without the event. --- **Censored** - observation ended before the full event path became known. ### Permanent trap Labelling every recently originated account as non-default because no default has happened yet. That converts lack of observation into evidence of good performance and biases event rates downward. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The statistical treatment of incomplete observation is universal; the underlying default definition may be governed elsewhere.

title: Selection, Survivorship and Truncation in Loan Books
one_screen: Loan books are filtered histories, not neutral samples. Approval, payoff, refinancing, sale, write-off, closure and data-retention rules determine which accounts remain visible, so statistical relationships can be distorted even when every surviving record is measured perfectly.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Distortion | Lending example | Direction of risk bias can be | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Selection bias | Only approved applicants have repayment outcomes | Usually makes applicant risk look safer than the full application pool | | Survivorship bias | Only currently active accounts are analyzed | Drops repaid, defaulted or exited paths | | Left truncation | Portfolio extract begins after some loans were originated | Early failures may never enter the observed sample | | Attrition bias | Customers leaving the bank disappear from later snapshots | Remaining customers may differ systematically | | Acquisition bias | Purchased portfolio lacks original underwriting fields | Missingness depends on source book | The critical issue is conditional observation. If inclusion depends on borrower risk or a downstream outcome, then sample averages and fitted coefficients describe the selected population, not automatically the population that generated the original applications. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Define cohorts from an entry event such as application or origination, then follow all permitted exits. Do not define the cohort from who happens to remain visible later. ### Never confuse [Selection bias] and [Survivorship bias] **Selection bias** - systematic inclusion or exclusion at any stage of sample formation. --- **Survivorship bias** - the special case where cases are visible because they survived long enough to remain in the observed set. ### Permanent trap Using a current portfolio snapshot to estimate lifetime borrower behavior without reconstructing closed and failed accounts. The snapshot conditions on survival and therefore changes the population being measured. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. These are statistical consequences of conditional observation, not jurisdiction-specific rules.

title: Reject Inference
one_screen: A lender observes repayment outcomes for booked applicants but normally not for applicants it rejected. Reject inference addresses this missing-outcome problem, but no statistical technique can recover rejected applicants' true performance without assumptions about how approval relates to risk.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism CR owns the credit approval decision. QNT owns the inference problem produced when that decision determines whose outcomes become observable. | Approach | Statistical idea | Main assumption or weakness | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Approved-only model | Fit only where outcomes exist | Estimates performance conditional on historical approval | | Reweighting | Give approved cases weights representing similar rejected cases | Requires observable variables to explain selection sufficiently | | Augmentation | Infer expected outcomes for rejects from a preliminary model | Can reinforce the preliminary model's errors | | Parceling-style assignment | Allocate synthetic good/bad outcomes within score bands | Strong assumption about rejected performance inside each band | | External outcome data | Link rejects to later bureau or market performance | Coverage and outcome definitions may differ | The missingness is usually not random. Low-scoring applicants are rejected precisely because the lender believes their risk differs, so treating rejects as if they were a random subset of approved cases is structurally wrong. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Reject inference is assumption management, not hidden-data recovery. State what makes the missing rejected outcomes inferable before trusting the result. ### Never confuse [Missing at random] and [Missing by credit policy] **Missing at random** - outcome absence can be explained without dependence on the unseen outcome after conditioning on observed information. --- **Missing by credit policy** - outcome absence is created by a decision rule designed around perceived risk, making naive missing-data assumptions fragile. ### Permanent trap Calling synthetic bad/good assignments "observed performance". They are model-based imputations and should remain distinguishable from realized repayment outcomes. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta.
