The identification problem is mathematical; lending and fair-treatment constraints on how models are used sit outside this atom.

title: Rare Defaults and Class Imbalance
one_screen: Default is often a rare event relative to non-default, especially in high-quality portfolios. That imbalance changes what accuracy means, how much information each event contributes and how unstable estimates become; a model can look excellent by predicting the majority class while learning almost nothing about default.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Consequence of rarity | Credit effect | | :--- | :--- | | Majority dominance | Overall accuracy can be high even with poor default detection | | Sparse-event uncertainty | Default-rate and coefficient estimates become noisy | | Thin segments | Some grades or bins contain too few defaults for stable estimation | | Threshold sensitivity | Small cutoff changes can move many non-defaults and few defaults | | Metric dependence | Precision changes strongly with prevalence even when ranking ability is unchanged | Rare-event learning is an information problem, not merely a data-volume problem. Ten million non-defaults cannot substitute perfectly for a small number of defaults because the event observations carry the information about how the default class differs. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Always interpret classification performance together with event prevalence. A metric that ignores class composition can hide failure on the event the credit model exists to distinguish. ### Never confuse [Rare event] and [Small dataset] **Rare event** - the outcome of interest is scarce relative to the other class. --- **Small dataset** - the total number of observations is limited. A dataset can be enormous and still contain too few defaults for a narrow segment. ### Permanent trap Using raw accuracy as the headline measure for a default model. In an imbalanced portfolio, a trivial majority-class rule can achieve impressive accuracy without useful risk discrimination. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Class imbalance is a property of the data-generating process, not the regulator.

title: Resampling, Class Weights and Prevalence Correction
one_screen: Resampling and class weighting change how strongly defaults influence model fitting; they do not change the true default prevalence of the lending population. The essential distinction is between altering the training objective to learn rare-event structure and altering the probability scale on which deployed predictions must be interpreted.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Technique | What changes | What does not automatically change | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Oversample defaults | More default rows or repeated default cases in training | Real portfolio prevalence | | Undersample non-defaults | Fewer majority-class rows used in fitting | Real number of non-default borrowers | | Class weights | Loss contribution per class | Observed feature values | | Synthetic minority examples | Local feature-space representation | Historical event count | Sampling can improve learning efficiency but can also distort estimated probabilities. A classifier trained on a 50:50 resampled dataset has seen a different class prior from a portfolio where only 2 percent default; its raw probability output therefore requires careful calibration before being read as portfolio event probability. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Keep an untouched evaluation sample at natural portfolio prevalence. Training balance is a modelling choice; deployment prevalence is an empirical property. ### Never confuse [Class weighting] and [Probability calibration] **Class weighting** - changes the fitting objective so some mistakes count more. --- **Probability calibration** - aligns predicted probabilities with observed event frequencies on the intended population. ### Permanent trap Reporting probabilities from a heavily resampled training set as if they were automatically calibrated to the live book. Better minority-class learning does not guarantee a correct probability level. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Resampling and weighting mathematics are universal.

title: Vintages, Cohorts and Seasoning
one_screen: Credit performance depends on both calendar time and account age. Vintage analysis fixes the origination cohort so loans are compared at similar seasoning, preventing a new book from appearing safer merely because its borrowers have not yet had enough time to default.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Time axis | Question answered | Typical distortion if ignored | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Origination vintage | Which loans entered under the same underwriting and macro environment? | Mixes changing policies and borrower quality | | Months on book | How mature is each account? | New accounts receive less opportunity to fail | | Calendar period | What macro conditions affect all active vintages now? | Confuses cycle effects with origination quality | | Observation horizon | How long is performance measured? | Compares unequal event opportunities | A fair vintage comparison aligns account age. Comparing Vintage A at 12 months with Vintage B at 3 months confounds underwriting quality with exposure time. Conversely, comparing different vintages at the same calendar date can reveal common macro shocks but not pure seasoning effects. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Compare like seasoning with like seasoning unless the purpose is explicitly to measure calendar-time effects. ### Never confuse [Vintage effect] and [Calendar effect] **Vintage effect** - difference associated with the cohort's origination conditions, underwriting or borrower mix. --- **Calendar effect** - condition affecting multiple active vintages at the same time, such as a macroeconomic shock. ### Permanent trap Calling a recent vintage "better" because its cumulative default rate is lower before it has reached the age at which older vintages generated most of their defaults. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Vintage and seasoning mathematics are universal.

title: Probability Distributions for Credit Events
one_screen: Credit data mix binary events, event counts and positive skewed quantities, so distribution choice must follow the data-generating mechanism rather than convenience. Bernoulli and binomial models describe binary default events under strong independence assumptions; Poisson can approximate rare counts; normal approximations require enough aggregation and weak dependence.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Distribution | Credit anchor | Key condition | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Bernoulli | One loan defaults or does not | One binary trial with event probability p | | Binomial | Number of defaults among n similar loans | Fixed n, common p, independent trials | | Poisson | Approximate rare-event count | Many opportunities, small event probability, weak dependence | | Normal approximation | Aggregated estimates or sums | Enough independent or weakly dependent contributions | | Right-skewed positive distribution | Exposure sizes or recovery amounts | Quantity bounded below with long upper tail | Credit portfolios often violate independence because borrowers share macro drivers. That is exactly why a distribution that works for independent coin-flip intuition can understate clustered default outcomes during stress. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Use a distribution because its assumptions match the credit process, not because its formula is familiar. ### Never confuse [Individual event distribution] and [Portfolio aggregate distribution] **Individual event distribution** - describes one loan or one event process. --- **Portfolio aggregate distribution** - describes a sum or count whose shape also depends on concentration and dependence across loans. ### Permanent trap Applying an independent binomial model to a portfolio where defaults cluster through common economic conditions. The count variance can then be much larger than the independent model implies. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Distributional mathematics is universal.

title: Sampling Uncertainty, Standard Error and Confidence Intervals
one_screen: Every observed default rate is an estimate from finite credit history. Standard error measures how much that estimate would vary across repeated comparable samples, while a confidence interval turns that sampling variability into a range generated by a stated procedure; sparse defaults make approximation quality especially important.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism For a large, reasonably homogeneous sample, a default-rate estimator can often use a normal approximation. When events are rare or counts are small, exact binomial or carefully chosen alternative intervals are preferable because symmetric approximations can extend below zero or behave poorly near the boundary. | Driver | Effect on uncertainty | | :--- | :--- | | More independent observations | Usually narrows standard error | | More observed events | Improves information about event probability | | Strong dependence | Reduces effective information relative to raw n | | Very small p | Makes symmetric normal approximations fragile | | Narrow segmentation | Can sharply widen intervals through sparse counts | ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Pair a point estimate with its uncertainty whenever finite default history matters. A difference in observed rates is not automatically a meaningful difference in underlying risk. ### Never confuse [Confidence interval] and [Probability that the parameter lies in the interval] **Confidence interval** - a repeated-sampling procedure designed to cover the fixed parameter at a stated long-run rate. --- **Posterior probability interval** - a Bayesian statement assigning probability to parameter values after combining prior assumptions and data. ### Permanent trap Using a symmetric large-sample interval for a grade with almost no defaults and then treating its neat endpoints as precise evidence. Sparse-event intervals are exactly where approximation choice matters most. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Sampling uncertainty is mathematical.

title: Hypothesis Tests, p-values, Power and Effect Size
one_screen: A hypothesis test asks whether lending data are sufficiently incompatible with a stated null model to justify rejecting it. The p-value measures extremeness under that null, while power asks whether the test could detect a practically important difference in the first place; neither replaces effect size.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Quantity | Meaning | Common credit mistake | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Significance level | Long-run false-rejection tolerance under the null | Chosen after seeing results | | p-value | Probability under the null of data at least this extreme | Read as probability the null is true | | Effect size | Magnitude of the observed difference | Ignored when large n makes tiny effects significant | | Power | Probability of detecting a specified real effect | Ignored when sparse defaults make tests weak | ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Statistical significance answers whether random sampling variation is a plausible explanation under the null; it does not answer whether the difference matters economically or operationally. ### Never confuse [p-value] and [Probability the null is true] **p-value** - probability, assuming the null, of observing a result at least as extreme as the one obtained. --- **Probability the null is true** - not supplied by an ordinary frequentist p-value. ### Permanent trap Treating "not significant" as proof of equality. A low-power test with few defaults may fail to reject large but poorly estimated differences. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Hypothesis-testing mathematics is universal.

title: Dependence, Correlation and Confounding
one_screen: Credit observations are rarely independent in the everyday sense: borrowers share employers, regions, products and macro conditions, while borrower variables also move together. Correlation measures association, confounding explains how a third factor can create or distort that association, and neither by itself establishes causation.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Structure | Credit example | Statistical consequence | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Positive correlation | Higher utilization and higher arrears tendency | Variables move together | | Negative correlation | Higher score and lower observed default rate | Variables move oppositely | | Common-driver dependence | Unemployment shock affects many borrowers | Loan outcomes become correlated | | Confounding | Income relates to both loan size and default | Apparent loan-size effect may change after controlling for income | | Proxy relationship | Region carries information about local economy | Predictive association need not be causal | Correlation can be useful for prediction even without causality, but causal language requires stronger design and assumptions. In credit models, the practical danger is to interpret a stable predictive association as a mechanism that will remain unchanged after policy, portfolio or economic conditions move. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Prediction can use association; causal interpretation cannot be obtained from correlation alone. ### Never confuse [Correlation] and [Causation] **Correlation** - statistical co-movement between variables. --- **Causation** - changing one factor produces a change in another under a defensible causal structure. ### Permanent trap Reading a regression or correlation coefficient as a policy lever. A variable may be predictive because it proxies another condition, so changing the variable itself may not change credit risk. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Dependence and confounding are mathematical concepts.

title: Linear Regression and Its Limits on Binary Outcomes
one_screen: Linear regression makes the statistical predictor concrete: observed outcomes are represented as a linear combination of borrower variables plus a residual, and least squares chooses coefficients that minimize squared residuals. Applied directly to a binary default flag, that machinery exposes its own limits - fitted values can leave the 0-to-1 range and error variance changes with the fitted probability - making a different link function necessary.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Object | Meaning in a lending regression | | :--- | :--- | | Intercept | Baseline fitted level when predictors are zero on their defined scales | | Coefficient | Change in fitted outcome for a one-unit predictor increase, holding other included predictors fixed | | Fitted value | Model's conditional mean estimate | | Residual | Part of the observed outcome not captured by the fitted value | | Least squares | Criterion minimizing total squared residual size | For a continuous target, this can be useful. For Y equal to 0 or 1, however, a straight line has no natural probability boundary and the conditional error variance depends on the probability level. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule A linear predictor is a useful building block; ordinary least squares is not automatically a valid probability model. ### Never confuse [Linear predictor] and [Linear probability model] **Linear predictor** - a weighted sum of inputs that can sit inside many models. --- **Linear probability model** - directly treats that weighted sum as a probability for a binary outcome, allowing values below 0 or above 1. ### Permanent trap Interpreting an OLS fitted value of 1.08 or -0.06 as a usable default probability. The straight-line model does not enforce probability bounds. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Linear-regression mathematics is universal.

title: Logistic Regression and Credit Odds
one_screen: Logistic regression keeps the linear predictor but applies it to log-odds rather than probability itself. This makes fitted default probabilities stay between 0 and 1 while preserving an interpretable coefficient structure; CR owns PD and scorecard construction as credit objects, while QNT owns this statistical estimator.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Quantity | Interpretation | | :--- | :--- | | Probability p | Chance of event on the model's defined population and horizon | | Odds | p divided by 1 - p | | Log-odds | Natural log of the odds | | beta coefficient | Additive change in log-odds per unit change in predictor | | exp(beta) | Multiplicative change in odds per unit change in predictor | The effect on probability is nonlinear: the same coefficient shift changes p most around the middle of the probability range and less near 0 or 1. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Logistic coefficients are linear in log-odds, not in probability percentage points. ### Never confuse [Odds] and [Probability] **Odds** - p divided by 1 - p, comparing event probability with non-event probability. --- **Probability** - p itself, bounded from 0 to 1. ### Permanent trap Reading beta = 0.20 as a 20 percentage-point increase in default probability. It is a 0.20 increase in log-odds; the probability change depends on the starting probability. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Logistic-regression mathematics does not change by jurisdiction.

title: Segmentation and Binning Decisions
one_screen: Segmentation decides which borrowers are statistically similar enough to model together; binning decides which ranges of a predictor are treated as having similar risk. Both trade granularity against statistical stability, and both can manufacture apparent structure when thin lending data are repeatedly partitioned until a pleasing pattern appears.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Decision | More granularity gives | Too much granularity causes | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Portfolio segmentation | Better fit to genuinely different products or borrower processes | Thin samples and unstable segment estimates | | Variable binning | Captures nonlinear or threshold-shaped risk | Small-bin volatility and overfitting | | Merge adjacent bins | More stable event rates | Loss of real local structure | | Monotonic constraint | Smoother, interpretable risk ordering | Can hide genuine non-monotonic behavior | | Missing-value bin | Explicit treatment of missingness | Can turn operational missingness into an unstable risk proxy | A cut point chosen after repeatedly inspecting the same default outcomes uses outcome information to optimize the representation. That is legitimate model development only if its optimism is controlled with validation and out-of-time testing. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Every additional segment or bin spends data. Granularity is justified only when the extra structure is stable enough to survive new lending observations and time periods. ### Never confuse [Segmentation] and [Binning] **Segmentation** - separates populations that may require different model relationships or treatment. --- **Binning** - groups values of one predictor within a modelling population. ### Permanent trap Forcing monotonic bins by repeatedly moving cut points on the development sample until the bad-rate pattern looks clean. That can encode sample noise as if it were economic structure. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Segmentation and binning mathematics are universal; CR owns how the resulting scorecard is constructed and used.

title: Weight of Evidence and Information Value
one_screen: Weight of Evidence converts each predictor bin into a log ratio comparing where non-defaults and defaults are concentrated; Information Value aggregates those distribution differences across bins. QNT owns these statistical transformations and their failure modes, while CR owns the credit scorecard built from them.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism For each bin, compare the bin's share of all non-defaults with its share of all defaults. A positive WoE under the convention below means the bin contains a larger share of non-defaults than defaults; reversing the convention reverses the sign, so the definition must be fixed before interpreting coefficients. | Pattern | WoE behavior | Interpretation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Equal shares of defaults and non-defaults | Near zero | Little separation in that bin | | Non-default share exceeds default share | Positive | Safer under this sign convention | | Default share exceeds non-default share | Negative | Riskier under this sign convention | | Very small event count | Extreme or unstable | Smoothing or bin merging may be needed | ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule WoE and IV are properties of a labelled sample and binning scheme, not timeless qualities of a variable. ### Never confuse [Weight of Evidence] and [Information Value] **Weight of Evidence** - one value per bin describing relative class concentration. --- **Information Value** - one aggregate number per variable summing separation across its bins. ### Permanent trap Treating a very high IV as automatic proof of a brilliant predictor. Extreme IV can signal target leakage, post-event information or over-fine bins that memorize the development sample. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. WoE and IV are statistical conventions, not jurisdiction-specific mathematics.

title: Multicollinearity, VIF and Regularisation
one_screen: When lending predictors contain overlapping information, fitted coefficients can become unstable even if overall prediction remains acceptable. VIF quantifies how much linear dependence inflates coefficient variance, while ridge and lasso regularisation deliberately trade some fitting bias for lower variance or simpler models.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Tool | Mechanism | Credit use | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | VIF | Regress one predictor on the others | Diagnose redundant linear information | | Ridge | Penalize squared coefficient size | Stabilize many correlated signals | | Lasso | Penalize absolute coefficient size | Shrink some coefficients exactly to zero | | Elastic net | Combine both penalties | Handle correlated groups while allowing sparsity | High collinearity does not necessarily destroy predictions; it destroys confidence that any one coefficient represents a separately identified effect. Small changes in sample composition can then move signs and magnitudes sharply. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Stable prediction and stable coefficients are different objectives. Collinearity can leave the first acceptable while making the second unreliable. ### Never confuse [Multicollinearity] and [Correlation with the target] **Multicollinearity** - predictors explain one another. --- **Target correlation** - a predictor is associated with the outcome. A variable can be highly predictive and still be highly collinear with another predictor. ### Permanent trap Using a universal VIF cutoff as if it were a law of nature. VIF is a diagnostic; materiality depends on whether coefficient stability, inference or only prediction is the modelling objective. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. VIF and regularisation mathematics are universal.

title: Decision Trees, Bagging and Random Forests
one_screen: A decision tree learns nonlinear credit rules by recursively splitting borrowers into increasingly homogeneous groups. A single deep tree is high-variance; bagging and random forests answer that weakness by averaging many decorrelated trees trained on resampled observations and subsets of predictors.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Mechanism | What it contributes | | :--- | :--- | | Recursive split | Captures thresholds and interactions without a linear form | | Depth control | Limits how finely noise can be partitioned | | Bootstrap sample | Gives each tree a different training view | | Feature subsampling | Reduces correlation among trees | | Averaging | Cancels part of the trees' idiosyncratic variance | | Out-of-bag cases | Provide internal predictions from trees that did not train on that case | ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule The forest gains stability by averaging imperfect, deliberately different trees; it does not become reliable merely because it contains many trees. ### Never confuse [Bagging] and [Boosting] **Bagging** - trains models largely in parallel on resampled data and averages them to reduce variance. --- **Boosting** - trains models sequentially so later learners focus on errors left by the current ensemble. ### Permanent trap Calling a random forest immune to overfitting. Deep trees, leakage, unstable data and poor time splits can still produce an ensemble that generalises badly. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Tree and forest mathematics do not vary by regulator.

title: Gradient Boosting on Credit Data
one_screen: Gradient boosting builds an additive prediction function sequentially: each new shallow tree is chosen to reduce the loss left by the current ensemble. It is powerful on tabular lending data because it captures nonlinearities and interactions, but learning rate, tree complexity and iteration count jointly determine whether it generalises or memorizes.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Control | Lower setting tends to | Higher setting tends to | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Learning rate | Require more trees, smaller steps | Fit faster, greater overfit risk | | Tree depth | Capture simpler local structure | Capture stronger interactions and noise | | Number of trees | Underfit if too few | Overfit if too many without control | | Row/feature subsampling | Add randomness and regularisation | Use more information per tree but less randomness | For binary default classification, boosting commonly optimizes a logistic-type loss, so the additive ensemble often operates on a score or log-odds scale before mapping to probability. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Boosting performance is the product of many small modelling choices; iteration count cannot be interpreted without learning rate and tree complexity. ### Never confuse [Gradient boosting] and [Random forest] **Gradient boosting** - sequentially adds trees to reduce current loss. --- **Random forest** - averages many decorrelated trees whose main role is variance reduction. ### Permanent trap Selecting the number of boosting rounds on the same data later used to claim final performance. That turns the evaluation sample into part of model tuning. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Gradient-boosting mathematics is universal.

title: Feature Importance and SHAP Attribution
one_screen: Feature importance asks which variables matter to a model in aggregate; SHAP attribution asks how the fitted model allocated one prediction relative to a baseline. Neither statistic proves causality, and correlated lending variables can make attribution depend strongly on the chosen importance definition and background distribution.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Quantity | Scope | What it can answer | What it cannot answer | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Split/gain importance | Global | Which variables trees used to improve fit | Direction for one borrower | | Permutation importance | Global | How performance falls when a feature is disrupted | Causal effect of changing the feature | | Mean absolute SHAP | Global summary | Average size of local attributions | Direct causal importance | | SHAP value | Local | Contribution to one model output relative to baseline | What would happen under real-world intervention | The attribution is conditional on the fitted model and the treatment of missing or unknown feature combinations. When predictors are strongly correlated, distributing shared information between them is inherently delicate. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule An explanation method explains the model's calculation, not the world's causal mechanism. ### Never confuse [Feature importance] and [Feature attribution] **Feature importance** - aggregate measure of how much a variable matters to model behavior or performance. --- **Feature attribution** - allocation of a particular prediction relative to a baseline across input features. ### Permanent trap Saying "income caused the prediction to fall" because its SHAP value is negative. SHAP states how the model used income relative to its reference, not what would happen if the borrower's income were externally changed. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Importance and SHAP mathematics are universal.

title: Train, Validation, Test and Out-of-Time Design
one_screen: A credit model must be judged on observations that did not participate in fitting or model selection. Training estimates parameters, validation chooses among modelling decisions, final test data estimate performance after those choices, and out-of-time design adds a harder question: does the relationship survive later vintages and economic conditions?
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Sample | Permitted use | Why it exists | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Training | Fit coefficients, trees and transformations | Learn model parameters | | Validation | Choose hyperparameters, bins, features or stopping point | Compare development choices | | Test | Final performance estimate after choices are frozen | Measure selection-adjusted generalisation | | Out-of-time | Later observation period | Test temporal robustness and regime change | Repeatedly checking test results and returning to model development contaminates the test set even if no row is literally added to training. Human selection has extracted information from it. Random splitting can still be useful for some iid questions, but credit data contain vintages, repeated customers and macro regimes. The split must prevent the same underlying information from leaking across partitions and should resemble deployment. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Every modelling choice consumes information from the data used to make that choice. Final evaluation must come from data not consumed by fitting or selection. ### Never confuse [Validation set] and [Test set] **Validation set** - used to choose among candidate modelling decisions. --- **Test set** - held back until those decisions are frozen, then used for final performance estimation. ### Permanent trap Calling a dataset "test" after it has been consulted dozens of times to tune features, bins or hyperparameters. Functionally it has become validation data. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Sample-splitting logic is statistical. MRM owns governance over validation execution and findings, not these mechanics.

title: Leakage, Overfitting and Generalisation Error
one_screen: A credit model can fail on new borrowers for three different reasons that must not be collapsed into one label: leakage lets the model see information it could not have at decision time, overfitting learns sample-specific noise, and regime change alters the relationship after development. All can create impressive historical results and disappointing deployment, but their remedies differ.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Failure | What happened | Credit example | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Target leakage | Predictor contains information created by or after the outcome | Post-default collection status used to predict default | | Time leakage | Future information enters an earlier prediction | Month-end bureau field used for a decision made mid-month | | Train-test contamination | Evaluation information influences fitting or selection | Same borrower appears across train and test with overlapping history | | Overfitting | Model learns unstable idiosyncrasies | Deep tree isolates tiny borrower pockets | | Underfitting | Model cannot represent real structure | Single linear effect where risk is strongly nonlinear | | Regime shift | Future data-generating process changes | New underwriting policy or recession changes borrower mix and outcomes | ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Every feature must exist at the prediction timestamp, and every performance claim must be measured on data genuinely outside the decisions used to build the model. ### Never confuse [Data leakage] and [Overfitting] **Data leakage** - unavailable or evaluation information enters model development, creating artificial signal. --- **Overfitting** - the model uses legitimate training information but learns noise that does not generalise. ### Permanent trap Diagnosing every OOT deterioration as overfitting. A clean model can deteriorate because portfolio mix or macro conditions changed, while a leaked model can look stable until the leaked signal disappears operationally. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Leakage and generalisation are statistical concepts.

title: Survival Analysis and Time to Default
one_screen: Binary default modelling asks whether an event occurs inside a chosen horizon; survival analysis keeps the timing information and can use accounts whose full future is not yet observed. It separates the probability of surviving beyond a time from the conditional event intensity at that time, making censoring part of the model rather than a reason to discard every incomplete account.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Quantity | Credit interpretation | | :--- | :--- | | Event time | Time from defined start to default | | Censoring time | Time observation stops without recorded default | | Survival function | Probability the borrower remains event-free beyond time t | | Hazard | Instantaneous event intensity at t conditional on survival to t | | Cumulative incidence | Probability an event has occurred by a horizon under the stated event setup | A censored borrower still contributes information: the borrower is known to have survived event-free up to the censoring time. Survival methods use that partial information instead of pretending the borrower completed the entire horizon. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Censoring is information about how long an account survived, not evidence that it was a non-default for every future horizon. ### Never confuse [Hazard] and [Cumulative default probability] **Hazard** - conditional near-time event intensity among borrowers that have survived so far. --- **Cumulative default probability** - probability the event has occurred by a stated horizon. ### Permanent trap Reading a falling hazard as falling cumulative default probability. Cumulative event probability can continue to rise even when the instantaneous hazard declines. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Survival-analysis mathematics is universal.

title: Credit Time Series: Stationarity, Trend and Dependence
one_screen: Portfolio default rates, delinquencies and application volumes arrive through time, so nearby observations can share trend, seasonality and serial dependence. Time-series modelling starts by asking whether the process is stable enough for past relationships to repeat; if not, trend, seasonal structure or differencing must be represented before lag relationships are interpreted.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Feature | Credit example | Statistical implication | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Trend | Defaults rise through a downturn | Mean changes over time | | Seasonality | Application volume repeats annual pattern | Fixed-period structure recurs | | Autocorrelation | This month's arrears resemble last month's | Observations are serially dependent | | Structural break | Underwriting rule changes suddenly | One historical process becomes another | | Stationarity | Mean, variance and lag structure stable enough over time | Past dynamics can be estimated more coherently | ACF measures correlation between the series and lagged versions of itself. PACF isolates the relationship at a particular lag after accounting for shorter lags, helping distinguish autoregressive from moving-average structure. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Do not interpret lag relationships until trend, seasonality and structural breaks have been considered; non-stationary level movement can create misleading autocorrelation. ### Never confuse [Seasonality] and [Credit cycle] **Seasonality** - pattern repeating at a fixed calendar frequency. --- **Credit cycle** - broader expansion and contraction in credit conditions that need not repeat at fixed intervals. ### Permanent trap Randomly shuffling a time series before evaluation. That removes the very chronological dependence and regime change the forecast must survive. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Time-series mathematics is universal.

title: Macro Conditioning and Rolling-Origin Forecasts
one_screen: Macro-conditioned credit forecasting links portfolio outcomes to variables such as unemployment, rates or economic growth while respecting the direction of time. IMP owns how forward-looking information enters ECL; QNT owns the statistical lag structure, forecast design and rolling-origin evaluation used to test whether macro relationships genuinely forecast credit outcomes.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Design issue | Credit consequence | | :--- | :--- | | Publication lag | Revised macro data may not have been known at forecast time | | Lag choice | Borrower stress may respond months after macro movement | | Regime dependence | Relationship estimated in benign years may change in recession | | Scenario extrapolation | Stress values may lie outside historical support | | Baseline comparison | Complex model may not beat persistence or seasonal naive forecasts | Rolling-origin testing preserves chronology: each forecast is generated using only information that would have existed at that historical forecast date. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule A historical macro model must be evaluated using the information set that was actually available at each historical forecast origin. ### Never confuse [Scenario conditioning] and [Forecast accuracy] **Scenario conditioning** - model response given an assumed macro path. --- **Forecast accuracy** - how close predictions made from information available at the time came to subsequently observed outcomes. ### Permanent trap Backtesting with revised macroeconomic series that were unavailable when the historical forecast would have been made. This creates look-ahead information even when credit outcomes themselves are correctly time-split. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The statistical mechanics do not vary; accounting use of forward-looking information belongs to IMP.

title: ROC Curves, AUC and Gini
one_screen: ROC, AUC and Gini measure ranking discrimination, not probability calibration. QNT owns how these statistics are constructed, why AUC has a pairwise ranking interpretation and how prevalence and sample composition affect interpretation; MRM owns thresholds, breaches, escalation and the governance conclusion drawn from the metric.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Move a score cutoff from strict to permissive. At each cutoff compute the true-positive rate and false-positive rate, then trace the ROC curve. AUC is the area under that curve and can also be interpreted as the probability that a randomly selected default receives a riskier model score than a randomly selected non-default, with ties handled by convention. | Metric | Measures | Does not measure | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | ROC curve | Sensitivity versus false-positive rate across cutoffs | Probability accuracy | | AUC | Overall ranking discrimination across cutoffs | Calibration level | | Gini | Linear rescaling of AUC | Economic value at one operating cutoff | ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Any strictly monotonic transformation of a score preserves ranking and therefore preserves AUC, even if the probability scale changes completely. ### Never confuse [Discrimination] and [Calibration] **Discrimination** - whether riskier outcomes are ranked ahead of safer outcomes. --- **Calibration** - whether predicted probability levels match observed event frequencies. ### Permanent trap Claiming a high AUC proves predicted PDs are accurate. The same ranking can be paired with probabilities that are systematically too high or too low. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. ROC, AUC and Gini mathematics are universal; MRM owns governance use of the resulting numbers.

title: Kolmogorov-Smirnov Statistic in Credit Models
one_screen: The credit-model KS statistic is the maximum vertical separation between the cumulative score distributions of defaults and non-defaults. QNT owns that empirical-distribution mathematics and why KS depends on score ordering, sample mix and finite-event noise; MRM owns any threshold, breach, escalation or remediation attached to the number.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | KS feature | Meaning | | :--- | :--- | | Uses cumulative distributions | Compares the whole score ordering up to each point | | Maximum gap | Focuses on the single strongest separation point | | Threshold location | Score where cumulative separation peaks | | Sample dependence | Thin defaults can make the empirical maximum noisy | KS is related to discrimination but is not identical to AUC. AUC integrates ranking behavior across the ROC curve; KS keeps only the largest difference between the two cumulative class distributions. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule KS summarizes the largest observed separation, not the entire discrimination curve and not probability calibration. ### Never confuse [KS statistic] and [Operational cutoff] **KS statistic** - maximum class-distribution separation observed across all score cutoffs. --- **Operational cutoff** - business decision threshold chosen for lending action; it need not equal the score at maximum KS. ### Permanent trap Treating the maximum-KS score as automatically optimal for approval. Business costs, capacity, risk appetite and class prevalence can make another operating cutoff preferable even when KS peaks elsewhere. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. KS mathematics is universal; MRM owns governed limits and escalation.

title: Confusion Matrix and Threshold Metrics
one_screen: A ranking model becomes a binary classifier only after a cutoff is chosen. The confusion matrix counts the four resulting outcomes, and sensitivity, specificity, precision and related metrics are different ratios built from those same counts; QNT owns their mathematics, while MRM owns governed thresholds and actions taken when performance breaches occur.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Actual / predicted | Predict default | Predict non-default | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Actual default | True positive | False negative | | Actual non-default | False positive | True negative | No threshold metric is intrinsically best. The useful metric depends on which denominator answers the business question: all actual defaults, all actual non-defaults, or all predicted defaults. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Every threshold metric must be read with its denominator. Two metrics using the same four counts can answer entirely different questions. ### Never confuse [Sensitivity] and [Precision] **Sensitivity** - among actual defaults, how many the cutoff captures. --- **Precision** - among cases flagged as default, how many actually default. ### Permanent trap Optimizing a cutoff on F1 and calling it economically optimal. F1 assigns an implicit balance to precision and sensitivity but contains no loan margin, loss severity or operational cost. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Confusion-matrix mathematics is universal; MRM owns governance around performance thresholds.

title: Precision-Recall and Discrimination Under Severe Imbalance
one_screen: Precision-recall analysis focuses directly on the rare default class. It is especially informative when defaults are scarce because precision exposes the false-positive burden created by low prevalence, whereas ROC coordinates normalize separately by each actual class and can look strong even when most borrowers flagged as risky do not default.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism As the cutoff moves, recall is the same quantity as sensitivity, while precision asks how concentrated actual defaults are among flagged cases. Plotting precision against recall therefore shows the trade between capturing more defaults and diluting the flagged pool with non-defaults. | Metric view | Denominator emphasis | Imbalance behavior | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | ROC | Actual defaults and actual non-defaults separately | Can remain visually strong with huge non-default population | | Precision-recall | Predicted positives and actual defaults | Directly exposes low positive predictive value | | PR baseline | Event prevalence | Falls as defaults become rarer | ### Where it sits ### Formula text ``` ### Permanent rule When the event is rare, report a metric that makes the false-positive burden visible; ROC alone can hide how thin the default concentration is among flagged borrowers. ### Never confuse [ROC-AUC] and [PR-AUC] **ROC-AUC** - summarizes true-positive versus false-positive-rate ranking across cutoffs. --- **PR-AUC** - summarizes precision versus recall and therefore changes materially with event prevalence. ### Permanent trap Comparing PR-AUC across two portfolios with very different default prevalence as if the numbers were directly portable. The baseline precision itself changes with prevalence. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Precision-recall mathematics is universal.

title: Calibration Curves, O/E, Brier Score and Calibration Tests
one_screen: Calibration asks whether probability levels mean what they say: among loans assigned similar predicted risk, do events occur at roughly that frequency? QNT owns calibration curves, observed-to-expected ratios, probability scoring rules and calibration-test mathematics; MRM owns tolerances, breach classification, escalation and remediation governance.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Tool | Calculation idea | Main limitation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Calibration curve | Compare average prediction with observed event rate by bin | Depends on binning and sample size | | O/E ratio | Compare total observed events with total expected events | Can hide offsetting segment errors | | Brier score | Average squared probability error | Mixes calibration and discrimination information | | Statistical calibration test | Compare observed departures with sampling variability | Large samples can flag tiny differences; sparse samples have low power | ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule A model can discriminate well and calibrate badly, or calibrate the portfolio average while being badly miscalibrated within important segments. ### Never confuse [Calibration-in-the-large] and [Segment calibration] **Calibration-in-the-large** - total or average predicted event level matches total or average observed level. --- **Segment calibration** - predicted and observed frequencies align across relevant risk bands, products, vintages or other groups. ### Permanent trap Declaring a model calibrated because O/E is near 1 for the whole portfolio. Overprediction in one segment can cancel underprediction in another. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Calibration mathematics is universal; MRM owns governed interpretation of test results.

title: PSI and CSI: Population and Characteristic Drift
one_screen: Population Stability Index and Characteristic Stability Index are bin-based divergence summaries comparing a reference distribution with a later distribution. QNT owns their logarithmic calculation, dependence on binning and statistical limitations; MRM owns monitoring limits, breach escalation and what the institution concludes from a PSI or CSI result.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism PSI is usually applied to a model score or population-level distribution; CSI applies the same mathematical structure to an individual characteristic. Naming differs across institutions, but the core calculation compares bin shares between a reference sample and a comparison sample. | Driver | Effect on PSI or CSI | | :--- | :--- | | Larger bin-share shift | Increases contribution | | More extreme relative shift | Log ratio magnifies divergence | | Different bin boundaries | Can materially change the index | | Tiny or zero bin shares | Can create unstable or undefined log ratios without treatment | | Large sample size | Makes small shifts precisely measurable but does not make them economically important | ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule PSI and CSI detect distribution change, not its cause and not automatically model-performance deterioration. ### Never confuse [Population drift] and [Concept drift] **Population drift** - distribution of model inputs or scores changes. --- **Concept drift** - relationship between predictors and the credit outcome changes. Input distribution can move while performance remains sound, or relationships can deteriorate with little visible input drift. ### Permanent trap Treating a PSI increase as proof the model is wrong. The shift may reflect a deliberate acquisition strategy, seasonality or benign mix change; performance and calibration must be checked separately. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. PSI and CSI mathematics are universal; MRM owns governed thresholds and escalation.

title: Statistical Comparison of Incumbent and Challenger Models
one_screen: A challenger is statistically meaningful only when compared with the incumbent on the same untouched lending observations, outcomes and horizons. QNT owns paired performance differences, uncertainty around AUC, KS, calibration and loss metrics, and the question of whether an observed improvement is credible beyond sample noise; MRM owns why challengers are commissioned, acceptance criteria, approvals and replacement decisions.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Comparison principle | Why it matters | | :--- | :--- | | Same cases | Removes portfolio-mix difference from the model comparison | | Same horizon and label | Prevents outcome-definition mismatch | | Paired predictions | Uses correlation between model errors rather than pretending samples are independent | | Multiple dimensions | AUC gain can coexist with calibration loss | | Confidence interval on difference | Shows whether observed superiority is statistically resolved | | OOT comparison | Tests whether the advantage survives later vintages and regimes | ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Compare models on identical cases and quantify uncertainty in the difference, not just uncertainty in each model separately. ### Never confuse [Statistically detectable improvement] and [Decision-worthy improvement] **Statistically detectable improvement** - performance difference is unlikely to be sampling noise under the comparison method. --- **Decision-worthy improvement** - gain is large and robust enough to justify operational, economic and governance consequences; MRM owns that decision framework. ### Permanent trap Choosing the challenger because its AUC is 0.002 higher on one holdout sample without checking paired uncertainty, calibration, segment behavior or OOT stability. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Statistical model-comparison mathematics is universal; MRM owns governance of challenger acceptance and replacement.

title: Lending Data Grain, Keys, and Row Meaning
one_screen: A lending table is meaningful only when you can say what one row represents. Before writing a join or aggregate, fix the grain, identify the key that should be unique at that grain, and distinguish customer, facility, account, payment, schedule, and snapshot records.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Use one mental schema throughout the pack: Here `loan_snapshots` has grain **one row per account per reporting date**. The key is therefore `(account_id, reporting_date)`, not `account_id` alone. Other tables have different grains: `customers` is one row per customer; `facilities` is one row per facility; `loan_accounts` is one row per account; `repayment_schedule` is one row per account per due date; `payments` is one row per payment event identified by `payment_id`; `customer_risk` is one row per customer per effective-dated risk record. `finance_balances` is the comparison source used only for reconciliation, at account and reporting-date grain. A key question comes before every calculation: if two rows share the business identifier, are they duplicates or legitimate repeated observations? Two `loan_snapshots` rows for the same account on different month-ends are expected. Two rows for the same account and same reporting date are a duplicate at the declared grain. The same logic protects monetary measures. If `outstanding_balance` is stored at account-month grain, any operation that changes that grain can change the total unless the transformation is deliberate. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule State the grain in words before writing the query. A key is correct only relative to that grain. ### Never confuse [Duplicate] and [Repeated observation] **Duplicate** - two or more rows occupy the same declared grain when only one should exist. --- **Repeated observation** - the same entity appears legitimately at different dates, events, or child records. ### Permanent trap Using `DISTINCT` to hide unexplained duplicates. It removes identical result rows but does not prove that the underlying grain or join is correct. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Row grain and key logic do not vary by regulator.

title: Selecting a Reporting Population in SQL
one_screen: A reporting query is first a population definition expressed in code. `SELECT` chooses the fields, `WHERE` decides which loan observations enter the analysis, and `ORDER BY` makes output order deterministic when the order itself matters.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Suppose the analyst needs active accounts in the August 2026 month-end snapshot with positive drawn exposure: The order of the written predicates does not create a business hierarchy; together they define the row population. Be explicit about inclusions and exclusions. A condition on a date, status, currency, or product can materially change the denominator of every later portfolio measure. Use parentheses when `AND` and `OR` are mixed so the intended logic is visible: For date-time columns, prefer closed-open ranges rather than assuming every row sits exactly at midnight. The general pattern is `timestamp >= start` and `timestamp < next_start`. `ORDER BY` controls presentation or deterministic ranking input; it does not define table storage order. Without it, the database may return rows in any convenient order. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Write filters so another analyst can state the resulting population in one sentence without guessing at operator precedence or hidden defaults. ### Never confuse [WHERE] and [ORDER BY] **WHERE** - changes which rows are included. --- **ORDER BY** - changes the sequence of returned rows without changing membership. ### Permanent trap Treating a query that runs as proof that the population is right. SQL validates syntax and types, not the business meaning of the filter. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. SQL filtering semantics do not vary by regulator.

title: Credit Classification with CASE
one_screen: `CASE` turns an already-defined credit rule into a derived field. It is ideal for delinquency bands, active or closed indicators, exposure bands, and other classifications where mutually understood business conditions must become executable row-level labels.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism A DPD bucket can be implemented directly from `days_past_due`: `CASE` is evaluated top to bottom. The first matching branch wins, so overlapping ranges can silently misclassify rows. Put exceptional states such as NULL first when they need their own treatment, then use non-overlapping conditions. A searched `CASE` can also encode flags used later in aggregation: The code owns implementation, not policy. TEC can express `days_past_due >= threshold`, but the threshold itself must come from the credit, impairment, capital, reporting, or jurisdiction-specific rule that owns it. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Make `CASE` branches mutually exclusive and collectively explicit for the values that matter, including NULL when it has business meaning. ### Never confuse [CASE rule] and [Business rule] **CASE rule** - the SQL expression that implements a condition. --- **Business rule** - the governed definition that determines what the condition should be. ### Permanent trap Using `ELSE` as a silent garbage bucket. If unmatched values are possible and important, label them visibly so bad source values do not masquerade as a valid final category. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. `CASE` mechanics do not vary by regulator.

title: Portfolio Aggregation, Distinct Counts, and HAVING
one_screen: Aggregation changes grain. A loan-level snapshot can become one row per product, vintage, delinquency bucket, or customer segment, but the analyst must choose the grouping columns and the counting unit deliberately or the resulting portfolio measures will answer the wrong question.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism To summarize August balances by product, join the account to its facility and aggregate at product grain: `COUNT(*)` counts result rows. `COUNT(column)` counts only non-NULL values in that column. `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` answers a different question again: how many unique customers appear. `WHERE` filters rows before aggregation. `HAVING` filters groups after aggregates exist: ### Where it sits ### Never confuse [COUNT(*)] and [COUNT(column)] **COUNT(*)** - counts every result row in the group. --- **COUNT(column)** - counts only rows where that column is not NULL. ### Never confuse [WHERE] and [HAVING] **WHERE** - removes source rows before grouping. --- **HAVING** - removes groups after aggregate values have been calculated. ### Permanent trap Counting rows when the business question asks for customers or facilities. The SQL can be correct while the denominator is wrong because the table grain differs from the metric grain. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Aggregate semantics do not vary by regulator.

title: NULL Semantics in Credit Queries
one_screen: SQL NULL means unknown or missing, not zero, blank, or false. Because comparisons involving NULL usually evaluate to UNKNOWN, missing values can disappear from filters and alter aggregate results without generating any error.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism This query does not return NULL balances: Rows where `outstanding_balance` is NULL are neither equal to zero nor unequal to zero in ordinary two-valued logic. Test missingness explicitly: Aggregation has its own NULL behaviour. `COUNT(*)` counts rows, `COUNT(outstanding_balance)` skips NULL, and `SUM(outstanding_balance)` ignores NULL inputs but returns NULL if no non-NULL input exists for the group. Do not replace missing financial values with zero merely to make arithmetic convenient unless zero is genuinely the correct business meaning. `COALESCE` is useful when a fallback is deliberate: NULL also matters in anti-filters. `NOT IN` can behave unexpectedly when the compared set contains NULL. A correlated `NOT EXISTS` is usually clearer for population exclusion because it asks directly whether a matching row exists. ### Where it sits ### Never confuse [NULL] and [Zero] **NULL** - the value is absent or unknown. --- **Zero** - the value is known and equals zero. ### Permanent rule Test missingness with `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`, and substitute a default only when the default preserves business meaning. ### Permanent trap Writing `column = NULL` or `column <> NULL`. Those predicates do not identify missing rows; they evaluate to UNKNOWN. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. NULL logic is an implementation concept, not a regulatory one. 0` not include NULL balances?" a="A comparison with NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN rather than TRUE, so the row does not pass the `WHERE` filter." />

title: Join Cardinality and Exposure Fan-Out
one_screen: A join does not merely add columns; it can change row count and therefore change monetary totals. Before joining loan tables, predict the relationship between the keys on each side and decide whether one input row should match zero, one, or many rows on the other side.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism A monthly account snapshot joined directly to a repayment schedule is a classic fan-out risk. One account-month row can match many scheduled instalments: If account `A100` has one snapshot row and twelve schedule rows, its August balance appears twelve times. A later `SUM(outstanding_balance)` is then twelve times too large even though every join key technically matched. Diagnose cardinality before trusting measures: The safe shape depends on the intended result grain. If the output must remain one row per account-month, first reduce the schedule to one row per account for the required period, then join that result. A one-to-many relationship is not inherently wrong; it is wrong when the output grain was supposed to stay on the one side. Many-to-many joins are more dangerous because both sides contain repeated join keys. They can multiply rows combinatorially and often indicate that the join condition is incomplete or that one or both inputs need aggregation first. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Predict result cardinality before joining, then verify row counts and key uniqueness after the join. ### Never confuse [Valid one-to-many join] and [Fan-out error] **Valid one-to-many join** - repeated rows are required because the target grain is on the many side. --- **Fan-out error** - repeated rows were created even though the target grain was supposed to remain on the one side. ### Permanent trap Checking only whether the join returned the expected accounts. All accounts can be present while balances are silently multiplied. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Join cardinality does not vary by regulator.

title: Joining Customer, Account, Facility, and Repayment Tables Safely
one_screen: Safe lending joins begin from the table whose grain matches the required output and add attributes only through relationships that preserve that grain. When a child table contains multiple rows per account, aggregate or rank it to the needed grain before attaching it.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism For an August account-level portfolio, `loan_snapshots` is the base. `loan_accounts`, `facilities`, and `customers` are one-row lookups along the account-to-facility-to-customer path: Now suppose the output also needs scheduled cash due during September. The raw schedule is many rows per account, so first reduce it to account grain: The `LEFT JOIN` keeps all August accounts even when no September schedule exists. The pre-aggregation ensures at most one schedule row can match each account. After the join, validate the intended account-month key and a control total. Those checks belong in the analyst query or test harness rather than in memory. ### Where it sits ### Never confuse [INNER JOIN] and [LEFT JOIN] **INNER JOIN** - keeps only base rows with a matching row on the other side. --- **LEFT JOIN** - keeps every base row and supplies NULLs when no right-side match exists. ### Permanent rule Choose the base table from the desired output grain and force every many-side input to the required matching grain before joining. ### Permanent trap Starting from whichever table is easiest to type. The starting grain determines what can be duplicated or lost later. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Join construction does not vary by regulator.

title: Month-End Snapshots and Point-in-Time Populations
one_screen: A snapshot table stores repeated observations of the same account through time, so point-in-time analysis requires an explicit observation date. Mixing dates creates a portfolio that never existed and can combine today's balance with last month's delinquency or vice versa.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism The simplest correct month-end query fixes one reporting date before any enrichment or aggregation: If the source can contain multiple intra-month dates but the task needs the latest observation in each month, derive that selection deliberately rather than assuming the calendar maximum exists for every account. One common shape is to rank observations within account and month: That pattern selects the latest available observation per account-month, which is different from demanding a specific contractual month-end. The business requirement must say which one is intended. Point-in-time correctness also means every attached attribute must be valid for the same observation date. Joining an August snapshot to the customer's current risk grade in a table that has since changed introduces future information into historical analysis. ### Where it sits ### Never confuse [Calendar month-end] and [Latest available observation] **Calendar month-end** - a specifically required reporting date such as 31 August. --- **Latest available observation** - the maximum date present for the account or period, which may be earlier or later than the contractual cut-off. ### Permanent rule Every point-in-time portfolio must have one explicit observation rule, and all later attributes must be aligned to that observation. ### Permanent trap Using `MAX(reporting_date)` over the whole table and calling the result month-end. It returns the latest date present globally, not necessarily the required cut-off for every account. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Point-in-time query mechanics do not vary by regulator.

title: As-Of Joins to Effective-Dated Data
one_screen: An as-of join attaches the version of an attribute that was valid when the loan observation occurred. It prevents future leakage by ensuring an August 2025 snapshot cannot see a customer risk grade assigned in 2026.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Assume `customer_risk` contains `customer_id`, `valid_from`, `valid_to`, and `risk_grade`. If periods are non-overlapping, match the snapshot date inside the validity interval: The half-open interval `valid_from <= date < valid_to` avoids double matching when one record ends on the same boundary at which the next begins. Some sources store only change dates, not `valid_to`. Then select the latest record on or before the observation date: This assumes at most one effective record for a customer at a given start time. Duplicate or overlapping effective periods must be treated as a data problem, not resolved by arbitrary ranking. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A historical observation may use only information effective on or before its observation date unless the analysis explicitly requires hindsight. ### Never confuse [As-of join] and [Current-state join] **As-of join** - attaches the version valid at the historical observation date. --- **Current-state join** - attaches whichever version is current now, regardless of when the loan observation occurred. ### Permanent trap Joining history to a dimension table that contains only the latest customer record. The query runs cleanly but rewrites the past with present information. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Effective-dated join mechanics do not vary by regulator.

title: SQL Date Arithmetic for Reporting Periods, MOB, and Vintage
one_screen: Credit analysis repeatedly converts dates into reporting periods, origination vintages, and months-on-book. The craft is less about memorizing vendor functions than about using explicit boundaries and preserving the distinction between a date, a month label, and elapsed tenure.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Use closed-open boundaries for reporting periods so timestamps at the next boundary do not leak backward: Vintage is normally the origination period, not the snapshot period. If the database supports date truncation, derive a month label from `origination_date`: Months-on-book measures elapsed month boundaries between origination and observation. Exact syntax differs by SQL engine, so keep the business definition stable even when the function changes. In a dialect with `DATEDIFF` by month: Date arithmetic breaks when strings are mistaken for dates, timestamps are compared to inclusive end dates, or day differences are divided by 30 and called months. A calendar month is not a fixed number of days. ### Where it sits ### Never confuse [Vintage] and [Reporting period] **Vintage** - the origination cohort to which the facility belongs. --- **Reporting period** - the observation period in which balance or delinquency is measured. ### Permanent rule Express reporting periods with explicit lower and upper boundaries, and define MOB as a calendar-period concept rather than an approximate day count. ### Permanent trap Using `BETWEEN '2026-08-01' AND '2026-08-31'` on a timestamp and assuming every 31 August record is included. Values after midnight can be missed depending on the stored type and literal conversion. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Date calculations may differ by SQL engine, but not by regulator. = start AND date

title: Window Functions over Loan Histories
one_screen: Window functions calculate across related loan observations without collapsing them into one aggregate row. Their power comes from three choices: which account history forms the partition, how observations are ordered, and which rows are included in the window frame.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism To compare each account with its prior reporting date, partition by account and order chronologically: `LAG` preserves every snapshot row while exposing the previous value. `LEAD` does the same for the next observation. Ranking functions such as `ROW_NUMBER` also operate over a partition and order rather than collapsing the data. Running calculations require attention to the frame. For a cumulative amount by account: The explicit `ROWS` frame says to include all prior physical rows in the ordered account history. Omitting a frame can invoke engine defaults that behave differently when order values tie. Window functions assume the ordering column can establish the sequence needed by the business question. If an account can have multiple records on the same reporting date, add a deterministic tie-breaker or first resolve the duplicate grain problem. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule For every window expression, be able to state the partition, the order, and whether tied order values can occur. ### Never confuse [GROUP BY] and [Window function] **GROUP BY** - collapses many input rows into one row per group. --- **Window function** - calculates across related rows while preserving the original row grain. ### Permanent trap Using `LAG` without a deterministic order. The database may return a prior row, but not necessarily the prior business observation you intended. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Window mechanics do not vary by regulator.

title: Delinquency and DPD Sequences in SQL
one_screen: Delinquency analysis is an ordered-history problem: each account observation must be compared with earlier observations at the same grain. SQL windows let the analyst derive prior DPD, roll direction, first delinquency, cure, and consecutive-state behaviour without self-joining the snapshot table repeatedly.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Start by exposing the previous DPD for each account: A first-delinquency date can be derived without collapsing the history by using a conditional window minimum: Consecutive delinquency needs an explicit sequence rule. One practical approach creates a reset group whenever the account returns to current, then counts rows inside each delinquent run. That logic assumes observations are regular enough that consecutive rows represent consecutive reporting periods. If a month is missing, row adjacency is not the same as calendar continuity and the gap must be detected. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A sequence metric is valid only if the observation order and cadence support the meaning of "previous" and "consecutive." ### Never confuse [Prior row] and [Prior period] **Prior row** - the immediately preceding record in the ordered data. --- **Prior period** - the required earlier calendar observation, which may be missing from the data. ### Permanent trap Treating adjacent rows as consecutive months without checking for gaps. An account with June and August observations has a prior row but no July observation. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. DPD sequence coding does not vary by regulator.

title: First, Latest, and One-Row-per-Loan with ROW_NUMBER
one_screen: Analysts frequently need exactly one record from a repeated history: the latest snapshot, first payment, most recent risk record, or preferred duplicate candidate. `ROW_NUMBER` makes that choice explicit, but it is safe only when the ordering rule fully determines which row should win.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism To select the latest snapshot for each account: For the first payment, reverse the order: The second ordering column matters when multiple payments can share a date. Without a stable tie-breaker, two equally eligible rows can swap between executions. `ROW_NUMBER` can also resolve a known hierarchy such as "prefer active source record, then latest update." It should not be used to conceal unexplained duplicates. If two source rows are supposed to be identical at the business key, investigate why both exist rather than arbitrarily assigning one `rn = 1`. `RANK` and `DENSE_RANK` are different tools: tied values receive the same rank, so filtering `rank = 1` may return multiple rows. Use them only when ties are intentionally retained. ### Where it sits ### Never confuse [ROW_NUMBER] and [RANK] **ROW_NUMBER** - assigns a unique sequence number even when ordered values tie. --- **RANK** - gives tied rows the same rank and may return several rows at rank one. ### Permanent rule Every one-row selection must have a business-valid ordering and a deterministic tie-breaker where ties are possible. ### Permanent trap Using `ROW_NUMBER` to make a broken key unique. Ranking can choose a survivor while hiding the fact that the source contains competing records at a supposedly unique grain. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Ranking mechanics do not vary by regulator.

title: Building Lending Queries with CTEs
one_screen: A common table expression turns a long credit query into named stages whose populations and grains can be inspected. The goal is not to make SQL look elegant; it is to make each transformation explicit enough that duplication, filtering, and aggregate changes can be tested independently.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism A month-end portfolio with September scheduled cash flow can be written as staged logic: Each CTE has a declared shape: `month_end` is one row per account for the selected date; `september_due` is one row per account; therefore the final join should preserve account grain. CTEs do not automatically materialize data or make a query faster. Many optimizers inline them, and repeated references may still be expensive. Use them first for correctness and readability, then inspect the execution plan if performance matters. Avoid creating dozens of one-line CTEs that merely rename columns. A useful stage should correspond to a real population, grain change, aggregation, ranking, or business transformation that deserves inspection. ### Where it sits ### Never confuse [CTE] and [Temporary table] **CTE** - a named result scoped to the statement and often optimized as part of that statement. --- **Temporary table** - a separately created stored intermediate object with its own lifecycle and physical behaviour. ### Permanent rule Name CTEs for the business stage they represent, and know the grain of each stage before joining it onward. ### Permanent trap Assuming a CTE fixes performance by itself. It improves structure, but execution cost still depends on the optimizer, data volume, filters, joins, and repeated work. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. CTE usage does not vary by regulator.

title: Set Operations and Population Differences
one_screen: Set operations combine or compare compatible query outputs by rows rather than by columns. In credit work they are most useful for stacking like-for-like extracts, finding accounts that appeared or disappeared between populations, and checking whether two keyed sets agree.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism To stack two monthly exception files while preserving every row, use `UNION ALL`: `UNION` performs an additional duplicate-removal step. That may be required, but it can also hide repeated rows that should have been investigated and usually costs more than `UNION ALL` because the engine must identify duplicates. To find July accounts absent from August, use a set difference where the SQL dialect supports it: A `NOT EXISTS` anti-join is a portable alternative and can preserve additional columns from the left-side population. `INTERSECT` returns rows present in both compatible sets. Set operations compare row values in corresponding column positions. The branches must return the same number of columns with compatible data types and the same semantic meaning. Matching technical types are not enough if, for example, one branch labels `balance` in local currency and the other in base currency. ### Where it sits ### Never confuse [UNION ALL] and [UNION] **UNION ALL** - stacks all rows, including duplicates. --- **UNION** - stacks rows and then removes duplicates from the combined result. ### Permanent rule Use `UNION ALL` unless duplicate removal is part of the business requirement, and make the semantic meaning of corresponding columns identical across branches. ### Permanent trap Using `UNION` to "clean" duplicate source records. The operation can conceal a grain problem by silently removing repeated result rows. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Set-operation mechanics do not vary by regulator.

title: Writing a Reconciliation Query
one_screen: A reconciliation query implements a comparison that has already been specified: which two populations should agree, at what grain, on which measures, and with what tolerance. TEC owns the executable alignment and exception logic, not the governance decision that defines the control.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Assume `loan_snapshots` must reconcile to a delivered table `finance_balances` at account and reporting-date grain. Start by aggregating both sides to the same key before comparing: The full outer join exposes three exception classes: only on the risk side, only on the finance side, or present on both with a measure difference. The tolerance `1.00` is assumed to come from the control specification; TEC does not invent it. Always reconcile counts as well as amounts. Equal totals can hide offsetting record-level errors, while equal record counts can hide value differences. Where currencies differ, align currency treatment before comparison rather than relying on a single net total. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Force both sides to the same key and measure definition before comparing them. ### Never confuse [Reconciliation specification] and [Reconciliation query] **Reconciliation specification** - defines what must agree, the grain, measures, tolerance, and control expectation. --- **Reconciliation query** - implements that definition and emits the exceptions or evidence. ### Permanent trap Comparing only grand totals. Two sources can have the same net balance while containing different accounts or offsetting errors. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Reconciliation SQL mechanics do not vary by regulator.

title: Implementing Data-Quality Checks in SQL
one_screen: A data-quality rule becomes useful to an analyst only when it can be executed against the real lending grain and return clear exceptions. TEC owns the SQL pattern for checking a supplied rule; DAT owns the governed rule, threshold, severity, and control lifecycle.
